entry.title: Approximate Counting for Mixed $p$-Spin Glasses in Weak External Fields via Cluster Expansion
entry.summary: We give algorithms for approximating the partition function $Z_N$ of the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) model and finite mixed Ising $p$-spin models with $p\ge 3$. The algorithms apply at a fixed margin below the second-moment threshold $β_{\mathrm f}$ with homogeneous weak external fields $|h|\leqρ_0N^{-1/4}$, for fixed $ρ_0>0$. For any accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and failure parameter $δ\in(0,1)$, they approximate $\log Z_N$ to additive error $\varepsilon$. The number of exact operations is polynomial jointly in $N$, $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $δ^{-1}$. The disorder variables have i.i.d symmetric distribution with unit variance. The failure probability is at most $δ$ plus an explicit disorder tail bound. This tail bound tends to zero under a finite fourth moment condition. Our approach builds on the cluster expansions of Aizenman--Lebowitz--Ruelle~\cite{ALR87} and Dey--Wu~\cites{DW23,DW26}. For higher-order mixtures, we retain hypergraphs using few vertices and evaluate their total weight deterministically through local spin averages and inclusion--exclusion. For SK, we impose cutoffs on the number of vertices of degree at least three and on the total number of edges. We estimate the retained sum using randomized color coding~\cite{AYZ95}. A lower tail control based on reverse hypercontractivity~\cite{MOS13} converts the mean-square approximation of the normalized partition function into logarithmic accuracy.

entry.title: Online Interval Selection with Binary Predictions: Optimal Consistency and a Continuous Robustness Tradeoff
entry.summary: We study online interval selection with binary predictions of membership in a final optimal solution. Requests arrive in arbitrary order; accepted requests may be revoked, but rejected or revoked requests cannot be recovered. With rewards proportional to interval length, the best consistency under finite strict robustness is $d=(3+\sqrt5)/2$ when both guarantees hold almost surely on each fixed input, including for randomized algorithms. A continuous lower bound forces consistency strictly above $d$ at every robustness budget below $4\varphi+3\approx9.472$, whereas our deterministic algorithm attains $d$ with exact robustness $\varphi^5\approx11.090$, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. Each held interval inherits a ledger recording positive prediction mass lost through irrevocable decisions. A tunable replacement cost gives a continuous family with exact consistency throughout and exact robustness on two parameter intervals, including $(C,R)=(25/9,10)$ and $(4,7)$. Randomization permits expected consistency approaching one with finite expected robustness, whereas almost-sure robustness forces expected consistency strictly above two at every finite budget.

entry.title: A Linear Kernel for Planar Semitotal Domination
entry.summary: A set of vertices $S$ in a graph $G$ is a semitotal dominating set if $S$ is a dominating set and every vertex in $S$ has a witness, that is, another vertex in $S$ within distance at most two. The Semitotal Domination problem asks whether $G$ admits such a set of size at most $k$. We study this problem parameterized by the solution size. We provide a linear kernel of size $358k$ on planar graphs, a result that adds to several existing linear kernels for other domination variants on planar graphs. Additionally, we show Semitotal Domination is $W[2]$-hard on split graphs, on bipartite graphs and on $t$-claw-free graphs, it is $W[1]$-hard on circle graphs.

entry.title: Tight Bounds for Randomized Generalized $k$-Server on Uniform Metrics
entry.summary: In the generalized $k$-server problem, each of $k$ servers moves in its own metric space, and a request $(r_1,\dots,r_k)$ is served once some server $i$ stands at the point $r_i$ of its space. We determine the randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary when every space is a uniform metric. With unit distances the ratio is $Θ(k\log k)$: we give a $(k+1)\ln(2k)$-competitive algorithm and show that for large $k$ every algorithm has ratio at least $\frac{1}{20}k\ln k$, improving the bounds $O(k^2\log k)$ and $Ω(k)$ of Bienkowski, Jeż, and Schmidt. When server $i$ pays $w_i$ per move, the ratio is $\exp(Θ(k))$: we give a $20^k$-competitive algorithm, which also applies to weighted $k$-server on uniform metrics. This improves the $\exp(O(k^2))$ bound of Bijoy, Mondal, and Chiplunkar and matches the $Ω(2^k)$ lower bound of Ayyadevara and Chiplunkar up to the base of the exponent. Both algorithms follow normalized weights exactly, through couplings whose expected movement is controlled by the decrease of the logarithm of the total weight. The lower bound hides a random permutation among the solutions of random permutation constraints, which split into small, well-separated components, and then forbids one position to one server at a time.

entry.title: Polynomial-Time Solvability of the Mixed Evacuation Problem
entry.summary: The mixed evacuation problem is a variant of the dynamic transshipment problem where there exist two modes of transportation and we allocate supplies to each mode of transportation in such a way that we can send all the supplies from sources to sinks within a given time limit. It is known that this problem can be solved in polynomial time when the number of sources and sinks is small. In this paper, we prove that the mixed evacuation problem can be solved in polynomial time with the ellipsoid method.

entry.title: Linear-Time FPT Rectilinear Planarity Testing of Series-Parallel Graphs
entry.summary: A planar graph is rectilinear planar if it admits a planar orthogonal drawing without bends. For series-parallel graphs in the variable embedding setting the best known testing algorithm takes $O(n^2)$ time. We show that rectilinear planarity of a series-parallel graph with maximum degree four can be tested in $2^{O(k)}\cdot n$ time, where $k$ is the number of degree-4 vertices; the planar embedding is not fixed. In particular, the running time is subquadratic when $k=o(\log n)$. Each node of the SPQ$^*$-tree stores the set of its admissible spiralities; we show that this set is a union of $2^{O(k)}$ arithmetic progressions of step two. All proofs are in the paper and are additionally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

entry.title: Differentially Private Preconditioned Power Iteration Method for Principal Component Analysis that Adapts to the Coherence
entry.summary: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA), we are given as input a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and an integer $k\leq d$, and the goal is to find the top $k$ right-singular vectors of $A$. We consider the setting where each row of $A$ is the private data of an individual, and we design an $(ε,δ)$-differentially private algorithm whose utility guarantee improves with the coherence of the input matrix. Prior works were either restricted to the case $k=1$ or ensured significantly weaker privacy protections. Our algorithm is based on a preconditioned variant of the power iteration method that is designed to significantly reduce the noise needed to ensure privacy.

entry.title: Uniformity Testing for the Monomer-Dimer Model
entry.summary: We study uniformity testing for the monomer-dimer model on a known graph $G=(V,E)$. Given samples from an unknown distribution $D_w(M)\propto \prod_{e\in M} w_e$ over matchings $M$ of $G$, we ask whether $D_w$ is the uniform distribution over all matchings of $G$ or is $\varepsilon$-far from it in total variation distance. Our main result is that, for every maximum-degree bound $Δ$, uniformity can be tested with $\widetilde O_Δ(\sqrt m/\varepsilon^2)$ samples, where $m=|E|$. We complement this with an information-theoretic lower bound for general graphs: for every pair of parameters $n\le m\le n^2$, there are graphs with $Θ(n)$ vertices and $Θ(m)$ edges on which every tester requires $Ω(\sqrt m/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. Thus, for bounded-degree graph families with $m=Θ(n)$, testing uniformity over the space of matchings has $\widetilde Θ(\sqrt n/\varepsilon^2)$ sample complexity, in contrast with the $Θ(n/\varepsilon^2)$ samples needed to estimate $D_w$ in total variation distance.

entry.title: An Unconditional Space-Approximation Lower Bound for Semi-Streaming Matching
entry.summary: We prove the first unconditional lower bound tradeoff between the number of passes and the approximation factor of maximum matchings in the semi-streaming model. Specifically, we show that any algorithm that outputs an $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation to maximum matching requires $Ω(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ passes for constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Prior to our result, such tradeoffs were proven only conditioned on a certain combinatorial assumption about the density of Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs. The state-of-the-art unconditional lower bound rules out any approximation factor better than $(8/9)$ in two passes but leaves open the possibility of a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for any $\varepsilon > 0$ even in three passes. We provide two different proofs of our result: the first proof uses the recent hierarchical-embedding framework of Assadi, Konrad, Naidu, and Sundaresan (STOC 2024) along with combinatorial constructions using Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs. The second extends the two-level Ruzsa-Szemerédi hierarchy of Konrad and Naidu (SODA 2024) beyond two levels and proves the corresponding communication lower bound directly by induction, rather than through a reduction to Index.

entry.title: An $O(n^{0.1537})$-Coloring Algorithm for 3-Colorable Graphs
entry.summary: We present a polynomial-time randomized algorithm that colors every $n$-vertex $3$-colorable graph with $O(n^{0.1537})$ colors. This improves upon the previous bound of $O(n^{0.1954})$ colors by Bansal, Huang, and Lee (SODA '27). To achieve this result, we introduce a new algorithmic framework for finding a large independent set from a solution to the vector coloring SDP. Combined with the (combinatorial) dense-progress algorithm of Kawarabayashi, Thorup, and Yoneda (STOC '24), this framework yields an $n^{1/6 + o(1)}$-coloring algorithm. Furthermore, we strengthen the SDP-based algorithm specifically for 3-colorable graphs to achieve $O(n^{0.1537})$ colors.

entry.title: Tiny Suffix Arrays
entry.summary: Suffix array and inverse suffix array queries on a text of length $n$ can be answered in $\widetilde{O}(τ^3)$ time using an auxiliary data structure occupying $O(n/τ)$ words, for any $τ\in [1,n]$.

entry.title: Query Complexity of Learning Axis-Aligned Partitions
entry.summary: This work establishes the query complexity of learning high-dimensional boxes in the exact query learning setting. Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points, labeled by a collection of $k$ boxes: the label of each point in $X$ is determined by the unique box containing it. A learner aims to exactly recover the labels for every point in $X$ given access to a label oracle. We consider three increasingly-structured settings. In the most general setting, there are no conditions on the boxes, and they may overlap. We show that CAL (Cohn-Atlas-Ladner 1994), a classical active learning algorithm, is minimax-optimal with query complexity $Θ(kd \log (n/kd))$. When the boxes are disjoint, we examine two regimes. In the large-$k$ regime, CAL remains minimax-optimal. For the constant-$k$ regime, an optimized variant of the Halving algorithm (Hegedüs 1995) can beat CAL by a $\log(d)$ factor. Finally, in the most-structured settings, the boxes correspond to the leaves of a constant-sized decision tree. We prove a tight query complexity of $Θ(d + \log n)$ that is additive in $d$ and $\log n$, generalizing a recent result (Black-Larsen-Mazumdar-Saha-So 2026) that establishes the query complexity of learning decision stumps.

entry.title: Computation-Friendly Compression of Matrices: Speeding up Linear and Boolean Algebra
entry.summary: Large sparse matrices---adjacency matrices of web and social graphs, feature matrices of machine-learning pipelines, the relations of graph databases---are routinely compressed to save space. Classical compressors, however, force the matrix to be decompressed before it can be used, so the space savings often yield a computational overhead. A recent line of work studies \emph{computation-friendly} compression: formats that are not only small, but let us carry out matrix--vector products, and in some cases matrix--matrix products, sums and closures, directly on the compressed representation {\em in time proportional to that compressed size}. This survey organizes that literature around the kind of redundancy each format exploits: spatial clustering of the nonzeros ($k^2$-trees and their variants), similarity between rows (Boldi--Vigna-style referencing and set-difference compression), repeated substrings (grammar compression), and dense bipartite substructures (bicliques). For each family we describe the representation, the algorithms, the theoretical guarantees and the empirical performance. Further, we show that the last three families are instances of a single general scheme, which we call a {\em sparse straight-line factorization} of the matrix, whose forward and backward substitutions evaluate right and left products in time proportional to the size of the representation, and that the product of two such factorizations is again one, which gives matrix--matrix products with a compressed output. An appendix reviews formats that must be decompressed (at least partially) before operating, for completeness. We close with a cross-family comparison and a list of open problems.

entry.title: Improved Quasi-Polynomial-Time Approximation for Maximum Independent Set
entry.summary: We give a deterministic quasi-polynomial-time algorithm for the maximum independent set problem. If an $N$-vertex graph contains an independent set of size $2^{-t}N$, where $t$ is an integer with $1\le t\le\sqrt{\log N}/12$, then our algorithm finds an independent set of size $2^t$ in time $N^{O(t)}$. This gives an approximation ratio of $N/2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N})}$ in time $N^{O(\sqrt{\log N})}$, improving on the approximation ratio $N/2^{Ω((\log N)^{1/3})}$ obtained by Lovett [Lov26]. A limitation of this form of analysis follows from the integrality gaps of Tulsiani [Tul09]. These gaps imply that a universal guarantee of the form $\operatorname{Las}_{R(t)}(G)\ge2^{-t}N\Longrightarrowα(G)\ge2^t$, at $2^{o(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})}$ levels, cannot hold over a range extending beyond $t=O(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})$. Thus, the exponent $1/2$ is the limit of this form of analysis, up to a factor of $\sqrt{\log\log N}$.

entry.title: From Linear to Polylogarithmic: Dynamic Submodular Maximization over Matroids
entry.summary: We study the problem of submodular maximization under a matroid constraint. In this problem, there is a monotone submodular function $f: 2^{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ and a matroid $M(N, I)$, accessible via value and independence oracles and the goal is to find the independent set $S \in I$ maximizing the objective function, i.e., $f(S) = \max_{I \in I} f(I)$. In the fully dynamic setting, the active ground set $N \subseteq N$ evolves through element insertions and deletions. The goal is to maintain a solution $S \subseteq N$ with $S \in I$ and $f(S) = \max_{I \subseteq N,, I \in I} f(I)$ after each update. Two approximation algorithms have been proposed to solve this problem: Dütting et al. developed a $(4+ε)$-approximation algorithm with an expected amortized update time of $O\!\bigl(\frac{k^2}ε \log k \log n \log^3 \frac{k}ε\bigr)$, and Banihashem et al. achieved a similar approximation with a better update time $O\!\bigl(k \log k \log^3 \frac{k}ε\bigr)$. However, these methods both become inefficient when the rank $k$ of the matroid is large (e.g., when $k = n^{o(1)}$). The central open question in this line of work is whether a fully dynamic algorithm with polylogarithmic update time exists. We resolve this question by presenting the first fully dynamic algorithm for submodular maximization over matroids with polylogarithmic update time. Our algorithm maintains a $(4+ε)$-approximate solution with expected amortized update time $poly(\log n, ε^{-1})$, where $n = |N|$. In particular, the update time is independent of the matroid rank $k$, thereby eliminating the dependence on $k$ and settling the open problem.

entry.title: Attention under Bounded Key-Query Similarity: Space Complexity and Transformer Anisotropy
entry.summary: A growing body of work on KV-cache compression aims to reduce the memory requirements of autoregressive generation. These methods compress the stored context while approximately preserving attention computation, enabling generation with reduced memory consumption. Almost tight theoretical results on the worst case space complexity of attention have recently been obtained, but they are achieved by instances where queries can be perfectly aligned with keys. This directly contradicts the observed anisotropy of the key/query geometry in real transformers. In particular, it has been shown empirically that key/query cosine similarities are small even for most correlated pairs, i.e., near-perfect alignment of queries with keys does not happen in practice. In this paper, we study the space complexity of attention approximation under the assumption that key/query cosine similarities belong to a small interval around zero, i.e., a query cannot align too much with any key. We give a nearly space optimal algorithm and a corresponding space lower bound. Surprisingly, the distribution of key/query cosine similarities in our lower bound exhibits the anisotropy property empirically established and studied in the literature. Additionally, we show that the simple uniform sampling algorithm is nearly optimal for a typical range of parameters, supporting its surprising effectiveness on real datasets.

entry.title: Order-selection Prophet Inequality (Almost) Goes I.I.D
entry.summary: We study the order-selection prophet inequality. A gambler knows the distributions of independent nonnegative random values, chooses the order in which to inspect them, and may irrevocably accept at most one value, at the time it is revealed. Since the order is irrelevant when the values are i.i.d., no algorithm can guarantee more than the optimal i.i.d.\ ratio $Γ_\star\approx0.74544$ of the expected maximum. We give an algorithm with competitive ratio $0.74500001$, less than $4.5\times10^{-4}$ below this bound. The algorithm samples independent arrival times and uses item-dependent thresholds. It is designed so that, conditional on its value, every item is selected with probability equal to a fixed fraction of its probability of being the maximum. We show that the constructions of this form that apply one local rule to every item are exactly those given by an allocation kernel, that is, by a coupling of two uniform random variables. Requiring every rarely winning item to follow the optimal i.i.d.\ threshold path singles out a baseline kernel, for which we prove analytically a ratio $Γ_0\approx0.7389$, defined through a one-dimensional control problem. Our final kernel perturbs this baseline, and its guarantee combines analytic estimates with a rigorous computer-assisted certificate.

entry.title: When is greedy exact for weighted minimum 3-cut?
entry.summary: The greedy algorithm for minimum 3-cut splits a global minimum-weight cut and then the cheaper of its two sides; it is a tight $4/3$-approximation. We show that it is exact, from every global minimum-weight cut, whenever some optimal 3-partition has two parts joined by total weight at least the weighted edge connectivity $λ$. This extends both theorems of Hochbaum and Shmoys from unweighted planar graphs to all weighted graphs, recovers the $4/3$ bound, and generalizes to minimum $k$-cut with a one-paragraph proof. The remaining hard instances have all pair weights below $λ$; for them we prove a merge lemma for Gomory-Hu sides. Finally, we give a 7-vertex graph with a unique Gomory-Hu tree whose unique optimal 3-partition contains no side of that tree, so the first stage of Kapoor's algorithm does not suffice on its own. The main theorem, the 4/3 bound, the merge lemmas and the counterexample are verified in the Lean 4 proof assistant.
entry.arxiv:comment: 16 pages. Lean 4 proofs and Python reproduction scripts are provided as ancillary files and at https://github.com/armandorodado/minimum-3cut. Submitted to Operations Research Letters

entry.title: Linear Hashing Is Poissonesque
entry.summary: The Poisson approximation theorem states that when $m$ balls are tossed uniformly and randomly into $n$ bins, the distribution of the bin loads can sometimes be approximated by $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. We show that when the balls are tossed via a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map, the load distribution is still governed by this Poisson distribution, albeit in a (necessarily) weaker manner. This allows us to show that a random linear map behaves like a fully random map in the following ways: 1. $\textbf{Expected loads.}$ We show that the expected value of the $r$th largest bin is governed by the $r$th largest value among $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. Specializing to the canonical setting of $m=n$ and $r=1$, our bounds show that the expected maximum load when $n$ balls are hashed into $n$ bins by a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map is no more than the corresponding expectation for a fully random map $\textit{plus}$ $\frac{3}2 + o(1)$. Specializing to $m\gg n\log n$, we show that the expected max load is $(1+o(1))m/n$ in this regime. 2. $\textbf{Concentration.}$ When $m\gg n\log (1/ρ)$ balls are tossed into $n$ bins randomly, we expect with $0.99$ probability that $\textit{every}$ density-$ρ$ subset of bins will contain a $(1\pm o(1) )ρ$-fraction of the balls. We show that this remains the case if the $m$ balls are tossed using a random linear map, and our bound matches the $o(1)$-factor produced by the fully random case. This gives a stronger version of the Leftover Hash Lemma for linear maps. An implication of this is that all bins have load $m/n \pm O(\sqrt{(m/n)\log n})$ with probability $0.99$. We obtain these results by showing that the average of a log-potential on the bin loads is upper bounded by the cumulant generating function of a Poisson random variable of mean $m/n$.

entry.title: The Complexity of Value Optimization in Sporadic Task Systems
entry.summary: Value-based Task Selection (VTS) asks whether a real-time system can select tasks whose total value reaches a required target while preserving every deadline. We study its threshold decision form for finite collections of independent sporadic tasks scheduled preemptively on one processor. We prove that this problem is $Σ_2^P$-complete for both constrained and arbitrary deadlines, even when all numerical parameters are encoded in unary. The existential choice is the selected task set, while the universal condition requires every processor-demand window to remain feasible. Our hardness reduction already uses constrained-deadline tasks. It represents universal assignments by Chinese Remainder Theorem timestamps and uses polynomial-weight local selector locks to enforce a valid existential assignment. The reduction produces polynomially many tasks, and every generated execution time, deadline, period, task value, and target is polynomially bounded in the source-instance size.

entry.title: Coordinating Boundaries: Improved Approximation Algorithms for Unweighted Non-Preemptive Throughput Maximization
entry.summary: We study unweighted nonpreemptive throughput maximization: given jobs with processing times, release times, and deadlines, schedule a maximum-cardinality subset on identical machines. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give randomized algorithms with expected approximation ratios $17/13+\varepsilon$ in polynomial time and $21/17+\varepsilon$ in pseudopolynomial time. These improve the respective $4/3+\varepsilon$ and $5/4+\varepsilon$ guarantees of Armbruster, Grandoni, Tinguely, and Wiese [STOC'26]. Both results hold for an arbitrary number of identical machines. Our algorithms build on their configuration-LP and matching framework, which partitions time into blocks. For a job whose window meets multiple blocks, its boundary blocks are the first and last such blocks. Crossing boundary pairs, whose endpoints strictly interleave, permit additional assignments to sampled execution slots, while a noncrossing family can be coordinated using consistent joint distributions on at most three blocks. The exchange analysis accounts for fractional job assignments that must be erased before inserting an additional job. For the pseudopolynomial implementation, we project configurations onto selected job identities and use separate configuration distributions with common placement marginals. This retains efficient pricing while enforcing the correlations needed for coordination.

entry.title: Unconditional Lower Bounds for the Fredman--Khachiyan Algorithms for Monotone Boolean Duality Testing
entry.summary: We prove unconditional lower bounds on the number of recursive calls made by the two algorithms of Fredman and Khachiyan (1996) for monotone Boolean duality testing, as a function of the explicit input size $N$. For Algorithm A we show a lower bound of $N^{Ω(\log N)}$ on the dual pairs $(\HH_k,\LL_k)$ obtained from the read-once family of Gurvich and Khachiyan. The proof lower-bounds the number of leaves of every binary decision tree computing the function by the modulus of its multilinear polynomial evaluated at a complex point of the unit circle. It therefore applies to every choice of branching variables and, more generally, to the class of two-child variable-restriction procedures whose terminal calls have polynomially bounded decision-tree complexity. On this family the number of calls is exactly $N^{Θ(\log N)}$. For Algorithm B, a symmetric specialization of the polynomial padding construction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa, with full polynomial blocks, yields at least $q^{(t-1)k-t(t-1)/2}$ calls, where $k=4t^2$ and $q=Θ(t^2)$; as a function of $N$ this is $N^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ along an infinite family. In an appendix we show that applying the padding construction directly to Algorithm A gives $Ω(2^n)$ calls on a dual pair obtained from an unsatisfiable $n$-variable formula, which is only $N^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ in terms of the input size. No complexity-theoretic assumption is used. The proofs allow every branching-variable choice permitted by the respective algorithm. They concern the original recursive procedures, counting every invocation separately, without sharing calls or adding positive stopping tests.

entry.title: Online Discrepancy of Sparse Random Vectors over Long Horizons
entry.summary: We study online vector balancing for independent sparse random vectors: each arrival is supported on a uniformly random set of $s$ of the $n$ coordinates, with nonzero entries equal to one (binary model) or independent random signs (signed model), and an online algorithm must sign each vector upon arrival. The prefix discrepancy is the largest $\ell_\infty$-norm of the signed sums up to the horizon $T$, the terminal discrepancy that of the sum at time $T$. For binary inputs with $2\le s\le n/2$ and $T=Θ(n)$, Altschuler and Tikhomirov showed that both are of order $\sqrt{s}+\log\log n$; they asked how the prefix discrepancy depends on the horizon and whether a matching terminal bound holds at every prescribed time. Over long horizons, the two differ. For every fixed $s\ge2$ and $c>0$, every online algorithm, even a randomized one that knows the horizon, incurs with high probability prefix discrepancy $Ω(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{α_s})$ for $n\le T\le e^{cn}$, where $α_s=(2^{s-1}-1)/(2^s-1)$. For $s=2$, quadratic Greedy matches this bound; for fixed $s\ge3$, we give an online algorithm with prefix discrepancy $O(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{1/2})$. In contrast, a deterministic algorithm that knows neither the horizon nor the failure probability keeps the terminal discrepancy $O_k(\sqrt{s}+\log\log n)$ at each prescribed time, with failure probability $n^{-k}$ for every fixed $k$, for $2\le s\le n/2$ (binary model) and $2\le s\le n$ (signed model); for $s=2$, quadratic Greedy itself does so. This answers their terminal question, and the same order is optimal for prefixes at all polynomial horizons $T\ge n$. The lower bound uses a finite safety game realized within the input law; the upper bounds use moments of elementary symmetric polynomials and, at terminal times, a $\cosh$ potential or a translated gauge with a Foster inequality at every state.

entry.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for Euclidean $(k,z)$-Clustering
entry.summary: We study the optimal coreset size for Euclidean $(k,z)$-clustering, where $z\ge1$ is fixed. Huang, Li, and Wu (STOC 2024) proved a lower bound of $Ω_z(k\varepsilon^{-z-2})$ for $\varepsilon\gtrsim_z k^{-1/(z+2)}$, matching the known upper bound up to polylogarithmic factors. For $0<\varepsilon<k^{-1/(z+2)}$, the upper bound $\widetilde O_z(k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2})$ remained unmatched. The previous lower bounds gave only $Ω_z(\max\{k\varepsilon^{-2},k^{(2z+3)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-1}\})$. We close this gap by proving a matching lower bound throughout $0<\varepsilon<k^{-1/(z+2)}$, including arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$. Together with known bounds, this determines the optimal worst-case coreset size as $$ \widetildeΘ_z\!\left(\min\left\{k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2},\,k\varepsilon^{-z-2}\right\}\right) $$ for every integer $k\ge1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$. In particular, the bounds are $\widetildeΘ(k^{4/3}\varepsilon^{-2})$ for $k$-median when $\varepsilon<k^{-1/3}$, and $\widetildeΘ(k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ for $k$-means when $\varepsilon<k^{-1/4}$. Our construction uses projection levels to encode four-wise independent signs, allowing $k$ centers to detect omissions regardless of how the retained points are reweighted.

entry.title: Bicriteria Approximate Navigable Graphs in General Metrics
entry.summary: We study approximation algorithms for constructing sparse navigable graphs in general metrics. Given an $n$-point metric $(P,d)$ and a parameter $α\ge 1$, an $α$-navigable graph is a directed graph $G=(P,E)$ such that for every ordered pair of distinct points $s,t\in P$, the vertex $s$ has an outgoing edge $(s,p)$ with $d(p,t)<d(s,t)/α$. The objective is to minimize the number of edges. Approximation algorithms for this problem were recently studied by Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026), and independently by Conway et al. (SODA 2026). These works show that the single-criterion problem faces a Set Cover barrier: an $O(\log n)$-approximation is achievable, whereas obtaining an $o(\log n)$-approximation is NP-hard. To obtain faster algorithms, Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten introduced bicriteria approximation, in which the output graph is required to be $α$-navigable, while its size is compared against that of an optimal $β$-navigable graph for some relaxed parameter $β\ge α$. They gave a fast matrix-multiplication-based algorithm that computes an $(α,2(1+\varepsilon)α)$-bicriteria $O(\log n)$-approximation in time $\widetilde O(n^ω\log Δ/\varepsilon)$, where $Δ$ denotes the aspect ratio and $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Our main result is a simpler near-quadratic-time algorithm with stronger bicriteria guarantees. For every constant $α\ge 1$, we compute in time $\widetilde O(n^2\logΔ)$ an $α$-navigable graph that is simultaneously an $(α,2α+O(1))$-bicriteria $O(1)$-approximation and an $(α,α+O(1))$-bicriteria $O(\log n)$-approximation. We complement the algorithm with a hardness result showing that for every constant $η\in(0,1)$, no polynomial-time algorithm can compute an $(α,2α-η)$-bicriteria $o(\log n)$-approximation unless $P=NP$.

entry.title: A Nearly Optimal Min-Cut Algorithm for Dynamic Streams
entry.summary: We give an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space algorithm for the minimum cut problem in dynamic streams, resolving the space complexity of streaming min-cut up to polylogarithmic factors. Ding, Garces, Li, Lin, Nelson, Shah, and Woodruff (ITCS 2025) obtained the same $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$ space bound for insertion-only streams, while prior to our work the best known bound even for unweighted dynamic streams was $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$, due to Ahn, Guha, and McGregor (PODS 2012). Our main technical contribution is an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space for-each cut sketch in dynamic streams, which may be of independent interest. The construction applies to weighted graphs under general $\pmΔ$ updates, a stronger model than the standard dynamic-stream setting in which weighted edges are inserted and deleted in their entirety. Despite this stronger guarantee, our algorithm is surprisingly simple and relies on very little machinery. We also obtain applications to minimum $\ell_p$-norm $k$-partitioning for every fixed $k$, weighted correlation-clustering evaluation for two clusters, and for-each cut sketching in balanced directed graphs.

entry.title: New Fault-Tolerant $(α,β)$-Spanners
entry.summary: We present new constructions of vertex fault-tolerant (VFT) $(α,β)$-spanners with substantially improved size bounds. Given a bound $f$ on the number of vertex faults, an $f$-VFT $(α,β)$-spanner is a subgraph of $G$ that preserves an $(α,β)$-spanner of $G- F$ for every fault set $F \subseteq V$ with $|F| \le f$. Most existing constructions of VFT $(α,β)$-spanners rely on a black-box sampling technique that incurs an exponential blow-up compared to their non-fault-tolerant counterparts. We develop two independent techniques for constructing $f$-VFT $(α,β)$-spanners that improve the dependence on $f$, reducing it to polynomial overhead. For every unweighted graph $G=(V,E)$ on $n$ vertices, stretch parameter $k$, and fault parameter $f$, we show: (i) $f$-VFT $(O_ε(k^ε), O_ε(k))$-spanners with $\tilde{O}(f^{exp(1/ε)}\cdot n^{1+1/k})$ edges for any $ε\in (0,1)$. For any fixed constant $ε$, this introduces a $poly(f)$ overhead compared to the non-faulty constructions of [Ben-Levy and Parter, SODA 2020] and [Chechik and Lifshitz, SODA 2026]. (ii) For any $δ\in (0,1)$, an $f$-VFT $\left(O_δ(\sqrt{k}),O_δ(k) \right)$-spanner of size $\tilde{O}(f^{1+δ} \cdot n^{1+\frac{1}{k}})$. Hence, it incurs a size overhead of only $f^{1+δ}$ compared to the above-mentioned non-faulty analogs. (iii) $f$-VFT $(k,k-1)$ spanner of size $O(k^3 \cdot f \cdot n^{1+\frac{1}{k}})$, nearly matching the lower bound $Ω(f^{1-\frac{1}{k}}n^{1+\frac{1}{k}})$ known for $f$-VFT $(2k-1,0)$ spanners by [Bodwin et al., SODA 2018]. The first result is obtained via a new adaptation of the Baswana--Sen framework to the VFT $(α,β)$ setting. The other two bounds follow from a highly involved analysis of a natural extension of the fault-tolerant greedy spanner.

entry.title: Random Deletion for Circuits in Regular Matroids
entry.summary: We study a simple random deletion algorithm to find short circuits in regular matroids. Given a regular matroid $M$ with $m$ elements, the algorithm randomly deletes each element independently with probability $1-1/m^{Θ(1/g)}$ where $g$ is the size of a minimum circuit, and returns the remaining set $R$ of elements. We establish the following results: 1. With high probability, $R$ contains no circuit and is therefore independent. 2. For every $α$-approximate minimum circuit $C$ where $α\geq 1$, with probability at least $m^{-O(α)}$, the entire circuit $C$ survives in $R$ and moreover, the minimum number of elements that need to be removed to make $R$ independent is $O(α\log(α+2))$. This yields an algorithmic proof that the number of $α$-approximate minimum circuits is $m^{O(α)}$, improving the previous known bound of $m^{O(α^2)}$ by Gurjar and Vishnoi, and resolving a recent conjecture of Khanna, Putterman, and Song. Our results yield two immediate applications. First, we obtain very simple RNC algorithms for computing the shortest circuit, and for enumerating all $α$-approximate circuits, of a regular matroid without computing the Seymour decomposition. Second, we obtain a randomized parallel algorithm to find a basis of a regular matroid under independence-oracle access. It uses polynomially many independence-oracle queries in $O(\log m)$ adaptive rounds and succeeds with high probability. This follows from the framework of Khanna, Putterman, and Song and the improved counting bound, and extends their result from graphic matroids to regular matroids.

entry.title: Engineering Lightweight Burrows-Wheeler Transform Construction on the GPU via Prefix-Free Parsing
entry.summary: The Burrows-Wheeler transform (BWT) is the core of many compressed full-text indexes and most read aligners. The fastest BWT constructions on GPUs need about $20$ bytes of device memory per character, which severely limits the texts that can be processed there. For example, on our GPU with 24 GB device memory, this is only about 1200 MiB. Prefix-free parsing (PFP) can be used to reduce the memory requirements of BWT construction algorithms in main memory. But, it uses hash tables and inverted lists which are not suited for GPUs. We show that PFP-based BWT construction can work with only sorting, scanning, and simple data-parallel procedures. This results in our GPU construction gpupfpbwt that on an NVIDIA RTX 3090, reduces the peak memory on an English text 11.9 bytes per character. There, it can processes 2108 MiB input files, which is 1.8 times larger than what the current state of the art libcubwt can handle. It is faster than or on par with libcubwt on eight of nine repetitive texts but 2.0 to 3.2 times slower on five of six non-repetitive ones, i.e., it provides a trade-off between required device memory and throughput.

entry.title: A Factor-6 Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanism for Cascade Position Auctions
entry.summary: Position auctions require assigning advertisers to positions and determining their display order. Under cascade behavior, earlier clicks prevent users from reaching later placements, coupling the click probabilities of selected advertisements. Existing methods achieve constant-factor welfare approximation and monotone logarithmic-factor approximation separately, leaving open whether both guarantees can be attained simultaneously. The difficulty is that welfare-preserving rounding need not maintain the monotonicity of individual click-through rates required for truthful bidding. We resolve this problem by developing a polynomial-time randomized mechanism that achieves a factor-6 welfare approximation and truthfulness in expectation for arbitrary public advertiser-position click probabilities. The mechanism optimizes a reach-weighted linear relaxation and converts its solution into feasible ordered allocations through matching decomposition, probability-bounded grouping, and calibrated attenuation. This construction compensates for cascade dependence and ensures that each advertiser's expected click-through rate equals exactly one sixth of its fractional click coordinate. The resulting identity transfers the monotonicity of the fractional allocation to the implemented mechanism, enabling exact incentive-compatible payments while preserving the welfare guarantee. The allocation lottery and payments are computable in polynomial bit time, with exact sampling in expected polynomial time.

entry.title: Approximation algorithms for identical parallel machine scheduling with assignment costs
entry.summary: We study non-preemptive scheduling on identical parallel machines in which assigning job $j$ to machine $M_i$ incurs the cost $c_{ij}=a_iw_j+b_j$. The processing times $p_j$ and the cost weights $w_j$ are independent, and the number of machines is part of the input. For every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and every deadline $T$ for which a schedule with makespan at most $T$ exists, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a schedule with makespan at most $(1+\varepsilon)T$ whose total assignment cost does not exceed the minimum under the deadline $T$. Using this algorithm as a subroutine, we obtain a polynomial-time approximation scheme for minimizing the makespan under a total cost budget whose schedules always satisfy the budget; this answers an open question for costs $c_{ij}=l_ic_j$ with $c_j$ independent of $p_j$. For the lexicographic problem, in which the total assignment cost is minimized among all schedules of minimum makespan, we obtain in polynomial time a schedule with makespan at most $1+\varepsilon$ times the minimum and total assignment cost at most that of a lexicographically optimal schedule; this improves the makespan guarantees of earlier algorithms for additive and multiplicative costs. For costs $c_{ij}=s_i+a_iw_j$, where $s_i$ is charged for each job processed on $M_i$, the same guarantees are obtained in quasi-polynomial time.

entry.title: Subgraph Isomorphism, Integer Linear Programming, and Lattices: A Linear Algebraic Framework
entry.summary: The subgraph isomorphism problem (SGI) asks a deceptively simple question: is a graph B found inside a parent graph A? Famously NP-complete and the subject of volumes of study, attempts to practically solve subgraph problems typically require specialized software or the focused application of problem-specific theoretical knowledge. Here we present a straightforward linear framework that neatly joins SGI to lattice theory and constrained satisfiability and, importantly, yields an easily implemented algorithm that naturally leverages consumer-grade hardware and off-the-shelf libraries to compete with state-of-the-art specialized solvers. We additionally show practical realizations in approachable settings, along with some benchmarks that reduce 6+ hour computations to seconds. Aimed at readability, we develop a series of computable algebraic invariants and demonstrate their application to familiar problems such as the Knight's Tour, with a focus on providing an accessible entry point for researchers in graph theory, abstract algebra, and students in general.

entry.title: Optimal Worst-Case Open Addressing: Braided Cuckoo Hashing
entry.summary: In this paper, we introduce braided cuckoo hashing, an open-addressed hash table that supports load factor up to $1 - \varepsilon$ (for some parameter $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$), while supporting queries, insertions, and deletions in worst-case time $O(\log \varepsilon^{-1})$, with high probability. This result represents an exponential improvement on insertion/deletion time over previous constructions, and disproves a conjecture of Bender, Kuszmaul, and Zhou that the product of worst-case query time and expected insertion/deletion time must be $Ω(\varepsilon^{-1})$.

entry.title: Acyclic 2-edge-coloured graphs: polynomial-time linkages and colouring hardness
entry.summary: A path or cycle in a $2$-edge-coloured graph is alternating if consecutive edges have different colours. These objects are natural analogues of paths and cycles in graphs, and even more so in digraphs. A well-studied class is that of acyclic $2$-edge-coloured graphs, that is, those forbidding alternating cycles. In particular, (acyclic) $2$-edge-coloured graphs generalize directed (acyclic) graphs (DAGs), but the complexity of problems on DAGs is much better understood than that of the corresponding problems on acyclic $2$-edge-coloured graphs. We investigate the complexity of two such problems, whose directed counterparts are well-known. Our first result is an $n^{O(k)}$-time algorithm for the alternating $k$-linkage problem on acyclic $2$-edge-coloured graphs. This problem asks for $k$ vertex-disjoint alternating paths joining $k$ prescribed pairs of vertices. This generalizes the directed $k$-linkage algorithm for DAGs. For every fixed $k$, this also yields a polynomial-time algorithm for finding $k$ internally vertex-disjoint alternating $(s,t)$-paths, solving an open problem by Abouelaoualim et al. from 2008. We then consider the alternating chromatic number of $2$-edge-coloured graphs, defined as the minimum number of parts in a vertex partition such that each part induces an acyclic subgraph. This notion is analogous to the dichromatic number of digraphs, where it is known that deciding dichromatic number $2$ is NP-complete even on tournaments. Our second result is that deciding alternating chromatic number $2$ is NP-complete on complete $2$-edge-coloured graphs. Equivalently, deciding whether a graph can be partitioned into two induced threshold graphs is NP-complete.

entry.title: Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time
entry.summary: We study the fundamental problem of PAC learning positive linear combinations of $k$ arbitrary ReLU activations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to the Gaussian distribution, in $L_2$ loss. We give the first fully-polynomial time algorithm for this learning task. Specifically, our algorithm draws $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/ε)$ samples, runs in $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/ε)$ time, and outputs a hypothesis that is $ε$-close to the target concept with high probability. All prior algorithms for this problem require super-polynomial time in $k$ or $1/ε$, or leverage strong well-conditioned assumptions on the weight matrix. On a technical level, our approach develops a novel boosting procedure of a ``weak'' learner that recovers the hidden weight vectors to constant error, in a list-decodable manner. To develop this ``weak'' learning procedure, we leverage implicit tensor computation techniques to construct a low-degree filtering procedure based on Hermite tensors of the target function. This procedure amplifies separation among (clusters of) weight vectors to learn each of them to constant error. We then argue that the same procedure can be used for improving the estimation of hidden weight vectors, using gradient descent-like updates on the Euclidean sphere. A crucial ingredient of our algorithm is a pruning approach that ensures only relevant vectors that approximate the hidden weight vectors at target accuracy are maintained by the algorithm.

entry.title: Compressed Boolean Matrix Multiplication using Bicliques
entry.summary: Boolean matrix multiplication is a fundamental operation in many graph-based applications, including web and social network analysis, information retrieval, and graph query evaluation. However, conventional sparse representations such as CSR}/CSC still incur significant space and time costs on large graphs. In this work, we introduce a method for multiplying Boolean matrices based on a biclique-based compressed representation that decomposes them into dense bipartite subgraphs, thereby capturing large sets of implicit edges. We first improve the iterative biclique extraction algorithm of Hernández and Navarro by introducing percentile-based parameter adaptation that dynamically adjusts its parameters according to the degree distribution, enhancing both extraction efficiency and compression ratio. We then extend the Schoor multiplication algorithm to operate directly on biclique-encoded matrices, thereby enabling a compositional form of multiplication where the output can also be represented as a collection of bicliques. Our experimental results on large real-world web and social graphs show that our approach achieves substantial reductions in space and computation time with respect to CSR/CSC-based representations. For example, using biclique extraction just as a tool to speed up multiplication (but retaining the CSR/CSC format) yields up to 34-fold speedups. Further, using the biclique-based representation for input and output yields up to a 10-fold reduction in space and up to a 290-fold speedup for matrix multiplication. These results demonstrate that our representation based on bicliques is both space- and time-effective to support an algebra of Boolean matrices.

entry.title: Logarithmic Separation between LZ77 and LZ-End and Grammar Compression
entry.summary: We show that there is a logarithmic separation between LZ77 and LZ-End, and between LZ77 and grammar compression.

entry.title: Low-Crossing Spanning Paths via Quasi-Uniform Sampling and their Applications
entry.summary: Given a set system (X, S), we consider the problems of constructing perfect matchings and spanning paths (also known as Welzl orders) of X with low crossing numbers with respect to S. Matchings with low crossing numbers were originally introduced in the late 1980s in the seminal works of Welzl [29, 30] and Chazelle-Welzl [7], who showed that any set system (X, S) with bounded dual VC-dimension d has a matching with crossing number O |X| 1-1/d , which is optimal. Low-crossing matchings and spanning paths have found several applications outside of their initial realm of computational geometry, including algorithmic graph theory, model checking, and game theory. In many of these applications, |S| is near-linear in |X|, which motivated the search for an improved construction for this regime. However, the proposed new algorithms provided only average-case bounds or sub-optimal crossing number guarantees for d $\ge$ 2 [5, 12]. We propose a new quasi-uniform sampling based framework. This allows us to obtain a simple algorithm with expected running time of __ |X| 2 + |S| $\bullet$ |X| , which improves upon the previous-best Our result has several immediate consequences, including new faster algorithms for constructing low-crossing spanning paths for set systems induced by balls, as well as for neighborhood set systems of graphs. Moreover, we get the first quadratic-time algorithm for combinatorial discrepancy, with nearly optimal discrepancy (up to a log factor), for bounded dual VC-dimension set systems. Beyond these applications, we believe that our idea could be applied to other algorithms that use the multiplicative weight update method.

entry.title: Proximity Theorem and FPT Algorithm for Minimum Group-labeled Matroid Bases
entry.summary: Let $M$ be a matroid, let $\ell:E(M)\to G$ be a labeling of its elements by an abelian group, and let $F\subseteq G$ be finite. A base is $F$-avoiding if the label sum of its elements is not in $F$. We prove that, for arbitrary costs, a min-cost $F$-avoiding base can be obtained from any min-cost base using at most $|F|$ exchanges. This resolves the weighted proximity conjecture by Hörsch, Imolay, Mizutani, Oki, and Schwarcz. Our main technical tool is to replace the assumption of Schrijver--Seymour Conjecture in Liu and Xu's earlier work with Kemperman--Scherk Theorem. The proximity theorem combined with approaches in earlier work gives an FPT algorithm that finds a min-cost $F$-avoiding base parameterized by $|G|$. We additionally give an FPT algorithm parameterized by $|F|$, answering a question of Hörsch et al.

entry.title: Structure and Exact Certification of Nonnegative Tensor Decompositions
entry.summary: We study the structure and exact certification of nonnegative tensor decompositions supplied through rational factor matrices. Every failure of minimality or essential uniqueness contains an irreducible positive exchange between $p$ supplied terms and $q$ competing terms. A dimension count based on the Lovitz--Petrov splitting theorem bounds the effective order of such an exchange, the sum over the modes of the joint factor-span dimension minus one, by $p+q-2$, and this bound is attained at every supplied length $R\ge2$. After eliminating ambient-row variables by the Farkas lemma, the resulting semialgebraic systems have fewer than $2R^2$ real variables. For input bit length $L$, this gives a deterministic $G(R)L^{O(R^2)}$-time algorithm that computes the nonnegative rank and an exact minimum-length decomposition, decides minimality and essential uniqueness, and returns exact witnesses when either property fails. The exponent is independent of the tensor order and the mode dimensions. For Lebesgue moment tensors, positive quadrature determines the nonnegative rank and the uniqueness behavior, and some rational length-$R$ inputs force a common field of degree at least $\lfloor R/2\rfloor!$ for any exact minimum-length output. As an illustration, an implementation resolves all 114 instances left inconclusive by earlier positive-scattering criteria, of which 95 are minimal and essentially unique and 19 are minimal but nonunique.

entry.title: Selection under partial information
entry.summary: The selection problem asks to find the $k$-th smallest element in a given set $X$. Its complexity is well-known to be $Θ(|X|)$ for every fixed $k$. We consider the poset selection problem where a partial order $P$ on $X$ is given, and the underlying order of $X$ is guaranteed to be a linear extension of $P$. This generalizes several variants of the selection problem studied before. Our main result is an algorithm that performs $O( k + \operatorname{OPT}(P,k) )$ comparisons, where $\operatorname{OPT}(P,k)$ is the minimum number of comparisons required for the input $(P,k)$. If $P$ is a rooted tree, we obtain an $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log (k / \operatorname{OPT}) )$ algorithm, which can be further improved to $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log \log (k/\operatorname{OPT}) )$ or $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log \operatorname{OPT})$ under mild assumptions about $P$. Our algorithms are based on the work of Kaplan, Kozma, Zamir, and Zwick [SOSA 2019], who used Chazelle's soft heaps [J. ACM 2000] to simplify several older results. We introduce a new soft heap variant, the weighted soft heap, which allows greater control over which elements get corrupted.

entry.title: Deterministic Incremental Triconnectivity in $O(\log^2 n)$ Worst-Case Time
entry.summary: We consider the problem of maintaining the triconnectivity in some biconnected graph G in the incremental dynamic setting. We consider updates in the form of edge insertions and edge subdivisions, and triconnectivity queries, i.e. queries of the form "are there at least three vertex disjoint paths between a and b?". All algorithms presented in this paper are deterministic. All queries and updates are answered in worst-case $O(\log n)$ time. By combining this result for biconnected graphs with a result of Holm and Rotenberg [SODA'20] we get an algorithm for general graphs with a worst-case running time of $O(\log^2 n)$ per operation. These algorithms represent an improvement of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(\log n)$.

entry.title: A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every $\ell_p$ Norm
entry.summary: We establish an $Ω(d)$ lower bound on the competitive ratio of convex body chasing in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\ell_p$ movement costs for any $p \in [1, \infty)$. Previously, the best known lower bound for general $p$ was $Ω(\max\{\sqrt{d}, d^{1-1/p}\})$, established by Bubeck et al. (2019); a linear lower bound was known only for $p = \infty$, realized by the standard construction of chasing faces of a hypercube. Our lower bound strictly improves on the prior bound for every fixed $p \in [1, \infty)$ and shows that the functional Steiner point algorithm of Sellke (2023) - which has competitive ratio $O(d)$ - is asymptotically optimal for every $\ell_p$ norm. Our lower bound is based on the recursive construction of Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani (2023) for metrical service systems, which gives a lower bound of $Ω(r^2)$ for requests of size $O(r)$ in that setting. We show that requests in their construction, each comprising a set of discrete points in a graph metric, can be mapped to the vertices of convex requests in a $(2r+1)$-dimensional vector space while approximately preserving movement costs up to a factor of $O(r)$, which establishes the lower bound.

entry.title: Combinatorial Minimum Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time on Dense Graphs
entry.summary: We give a combinatorial algorithm that computes an exact minimum-cost flow in $n^{2+o(1)}$ time. This is the first combinatorial improvement since Goldberg-Tarjan [GT87], and is almost optimal in dense graphs. All previous faster algorithms, including the almost-linear-time algorithm of Chen et al. [CKL+22], rely on interior-point methods. Our main conceptual contribution is a black-box reduction from exact minimum-cost flow on general graphs to its approximation on DAGs, with only an $n^{o(1)}$ loss on the running time. This reduction allows future work on combinatorial minimum-cost flow to focus on DAGs, typically much easier to handle than general graphs. Our $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm follows by combining this reduction with a simple augmenting-path-based approximation algorithm on DAGs. The reduction is based on a new structural result, called a flow-cost-preserving DAG projection. Given an arbitrary directed graph, this construction produces a DAG that approximately preserves both the congestion of flows and their cost up to a small loss.

entry.title: Single-Machine Guarantees on Unrelated Machines and Beyond: Proportional Fairness for Nonclairvoyant Polytope Scheduling
entry.summary: The Polytope Scheduling Problem (PSP) is a general framework for preemptive scheduling in which feasible instantaneous job allocations form a packing polytope. In the nonclairvoyant online setting, Proportional Fairness (PF), a practical allocation rule rooted in market theory, is the leading general-purpose algorithm. On a single machine, PF coincides with weighted Round-Robin, which is $2$-competitive for weighted completion time with uniform release dates (optimal for nonclairvoyant algorithms) and $(2+\varepsilon)$-speed $O(1/\varepsilon)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Known guarantees beyond a single machine are weaker. This raises a central question: Are these heterogeneous environments intrinsically harder than a single machine under nonclairvoyance? We show that they are not: PF retains both single-machine guarantees on the novel class of support-submodular polytopes, which includes unrelated machines and polymatroids. On unrelated machines, this refutes a belief (JACM'18, SODA'25) that PF is not $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Our main technical contribution is an equivalent characterization: a polytope is support submodular if and only if, for all job weights, the optimal weighted completion time is concave in the processing requirements. This structural insight underlies both guarantees. For general PSP, the picture changes: we give the first lower bound above $2$, showing that every randomized nonclairvoyant algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least $2+10^{-5}$ for weighted completion time, even with uniform release dates. On the positive side, we substantially improve the best known guarantee for weighted completion time from $27$ (SICOMP'26) to $4$ via a new dual-fitting analysis of PF. For weighted flow time, we show that PF achieves the first $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive nonclairvoyant guarantee for graph scheduling.

entry.title: Pareto-optimal Scheduling with Predictions
entry.summary: We study preemptive single-machine scheduling with predictions, where a prediction of the order of the jobs (or of their sizes) is available, and the objective is to minimize the total completion time. An algorithm is $c$-consistent if it is $c$-competitive when the prediction is correct, and $R$-robust if it is $R$-competitive whatever the prediction. Since the introduction of this problem as one of the first examples of learning-augmented algorithms, the best possible trade-off between consistency and robustness has remained open. We determine it exactly for deterministic algorithms. For every $R>2$, we give an $R$-robust algorithm whose consistency is \[ c(R)=R\Big(1-\Big(1-\frac{R+2}{R^2}\Big)^{\frac R{R+2}}\Big), \] and we prove that no deterministic $R$-robust algorithm, with either predicted order or predicted job sizes, has better consistency. In particular, consistency $1+\eps$ is achievable with robustness $\eps^{-1/2}+\frac16+O(\sqrt\eps)$, whereas all previous algorithms required robustness $Θ(1/\eps)$. Our algorithm is greedy: it follows the predicted order as fast as possible, subject to the invariant that the cost paid so far is at most $R$ times the optimum of the instance in which every unfinished job would end immediately. The matching lower bound rests on the observation that every robust deterministic algorithm must satisfy the same invariant along its run on correct predictions.

entry.title: Tightening the Online Bin Packing Gap from Both Sides, and the Limits of the Current Methods
entry.summary: The asymptotic competitive ratio of online bin packing has been bracketed since 2018 by the lower bound 1.54278 of Balogh, Bekesi, Dosa, Epstein and Levin and the upper bound 1.57829 of their Advanced Harmonic algorithm. We revisit both sides with exact rational computation and prove what the computations say. On the upper bound, we rebuild the certification of Advanced Harmonic as an exact optimization over its dual parameters; with the published parameters this already certifies a ratio strictly below the published one, and re-tuning the algorithm's proportion parameters gives a certified ratio of 1.5782147437 (an exact rational), independently re-verified on all 402 scenarios. To our knowledge this is the first movement of the upper bound since 2018. On the lower bound, we prove that the 2018 adversary construction is rigid: extending it by any finite number of new batches of ordinary size (outside the window of sizes s with 2s > 1 and rational part at most 0.64819), placed anywhere, with counts depending on the observed statistics, adaptive or not, never improves the bound at any truncation level. The load-bearing fact is that the construction is volume-tight at every stop. A single window-sized batch added to the truncation-3 tree is shown by machine-verified certificates to leave its value below the published limit. A computational map covers the remaining natural extensions: unions of structural variants, two-statistic multi-batch adversaries, and three families of adaptive conditions that the paper's separation theorem allows but never uses; none improves the bound. On the algorithm side we show that the marking, bonus-item and red-sand mechanisms of Extreme Harmonic bind nowhere in Advanced Harmonic, whose bottleneck is a two-medium-item bin that no known mechanism targets. We record two corrections to commonly cited numbers.

entry.title: Exact Algorithms and Complexity of the Smallest Grammar Problem
entry.summary: The Smallest Grammar Problem (SGP) asks for a smallest straight-line grammar generating a given string, with size measured by the total right-hand-side length. For an input of length $n\ge2$ over at most $σ$ symbols, where $2\leσ\le n$, let $R=\log_σn$. We give a deterministic exact algorithm running in $n^{O(1)}2^{O(n\log\log n/(R\sqrt{\log n}))}$ time and polynomial space, with constants independent of $σ$. This gives time $2^{O(n\log\log n/(\log n)^{3/2})}$ for fixed alphabets and $2^{O(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ for arbitrary alphabets, up to polynomial factors. The algorithm combines pairwise disjoint representative occurrences of dictionary strings, a sparse interval certificate, and the Boolean tensor contraction theorem of OpenAI. It explicitly enforces dictionary membership, rule boundaries, and the grammar-size budget. Independently of that contraction theorem, disjoint representatives yield exact algorithms in $O^*(1.872258^n)$ time and $2^{O((n/R)\log(R+1))}$ time using $O(n)$ words of space. Anchor-based grammar projections establish binary NP-completeness and reductions with tunable alphabet size. We state their consequences as unconditional quantitative transfers from SGP algorithms to sparse SAT algorithms, and quantify the additional loss from sparsifying general formulas.

entry.title: The Exact Robustness of Smith's Rule with Predicted Processing Times
entry.summary: Smith's rule orders jobs by their weight-to-processing-time ratios. We study the robustness of its list schedule on identical parallel machines when job $j$ is ordered using a nominal processing time $μ_j$ and its true processing time satisfies $μ_j\leq p_j\leqαμ_j$, where $α\geq1$. We determine the exact worst-case approximation ratio against the clairvoyant optimum, taking the supremum over machine counts. The ratio is an explicit continuous piecewise-algebraic function of $α$. It equals the Kawaguchi--Kyan constant $(1+\sqrt{2})/2$ at $α=1$ and is exactly $\sqrtα$ for $α\geq4$. On one machine the exact ratio is $\sqrtα$. For every fixed machine count, no deterministic nonpreemptive algorithm can improve on this guarantee, even with knowledge of $α$. The proof reduces to a common nominal Smith ratio and endpoint errors. Cutting the list schedule at its minimum final machine load yields a prefix--suffix certificate; two packings of matching lower-bound instances explain the branches below $α=4$. We also prove a nominal-to-robust transfer: any fixed schedule ordered by nominal Smith ratios on each machine, with nominal approximation ratio $1+δ$, has realized ratio at most $\sqrtα+αδ$. A nominal approximation scheme then gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm independent of $α$ with ratio $(1+\varepsilon)\sqrtα$ simultaneously for $1\leqα\leq4$.

entry.title: Beyond 3SUM-Hardness for Geometric Problems
entry.summary: Since the early days of fine-grained complexity, many geometric problems have been shown to require quadratic time under the 3SUM Hypothesis. But as the 3SUM Hypothesis was recently refuted, these lower bounds have lost their foundation. In this note we point out that many of them can be recovered under an alternative hardness assumption, the $k$-AP Hypothesis. The required changes to the proofs are trivial, so the lower bounds remain just as easy to teach.

entry.title: Efficient and Optimal Learning of Discrete Distributions with Person-Level Privacy
entry.summary: We study learning a discrete distribution under person-level differential privacy in the batched setting. Given $n$ users, each contributing $m$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $μ$ over $[k]$, we seek an estimate of $μ$ with total-variation error $α$. We give polynomial-time algorithms under both pure and approximate differential privacy. Under pure $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k/\varepsilon)$, the first polynomial-time pure-DP guarantee matching the information-theoretic optimum up to logarithmic factors. Under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k+\log(1/δ)/\varepsilon)$. At $δ=2^{-Θ(k)}$, this is $\widetilde O(k)$ for fixed $α,\varepsilon,m$ and failure probability. Our algorithms use a new degree-6 sum-of-squares estimator for learning from untrusted batches. Its key ingredient is a trace-bounded diagonal majorizer for the difference between the empirical covariance of the repaired batch averages and the multinomial covariance predicted by their mean. We prove that clean data admit this certificate through semidefinite-programming duality and a new application of the stronger symmetric form of Grothendieck's inequality due to Friedland and Lim. The certificate preserves the mean-dependent variance of multinomial batch averages, yielding the near-optimal robust rate $O(η\sqrt{\log(1/η)/m})$ and providing the score required by the privacy reduction. We also prove a statistical query lower bound ruling out a uniformly smaller order of error under fixed polynomial SQ resource bounds.

entry.title: Closing All-Exp Gaps in Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem and Maximum Constraint Assignment
entry.summary: We prove the all-exp property for the Traveling Salesman Problem with the $2$-opt neighborhood, and for $(3,2,2)$- and $(2,3,2)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment with the flip neighborhood. The all-exp property states that infinitely many instances have an initial solution from which every sequence of improving moves to a local optimum, and hence every run of local search, has exponential length. For the Traveling Salesman Problem, the all-exp property was previously known for every $k$-opt neighborhood with $k \ge 3$, so our result for $2$-opt completes the picture for all $k$-kopt neighborhoods. In $(p,q,r)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment, each constraint involves at most $p$ variables, each variable occurs in at most $q$ constraints, and each domain has size $r$. Decreasing any of the parameters of $(3,2,2)$ or $(2,3,2)$ yields a problem in which every sequence of improving flips has polynomial length, so both Maximum Constraint Assignment results are tight. All three results settle long-standing open problems. Our proofs build on a common construction idea, which reveals a close connection between the local-search dynamics of the three problems.

entry.title: Coresets for $k$-Means: When Does Uniform Sampling Suffice?
entry.summary: Data summarization techniques, such as coresets, are essential for scaling clustering algorithms to massive datasets. We study uniform sampling, which is an extremely simple and ultra-efficient method to construct coresets, in the context of weak, stable, and strong coresets for the $k$-means problem in Hilbert space. We begin with the fundamental case $k=1$, and establish matching upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of stable and weak coresets, finding that the two notions require different sample complexities. As a consequence, we obtain tight bounds for stable $1$-median coresets in $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ (and thus also Kendall--tau and Jaccard metrics), removing the dimension dependence of Carmel and Krauthgamer (ICLR 2026). Our analysis is substantially simpler than prior work and reduces to bounding the deviation of the sample mean. For the general $k$-means problem on $ρ$-separated instances, a well-studied structural assumption on the input, we show that uniform sampling yields a stable coreset for all $O(1)$-approximate solutions, and a strong coreset if the instance additionally has bounded kurtosis. In all these results, the sample complexity is independent of the dimension and the instance size.

entry.title: Peak-Aware One-Way Trading: Competitive and Learning-Augmented Algorithms for Energy Procurement
entry.summary: We introduce peak-aware one-way trading ($\texttt{PA-OWT}$), an online problem in which a player must purchase a fixed quantity of an asset by a deadline, minimizing its total cost plus a charge proportional to the largest single purchase at any time. The model is motivated by electricity procurement, where the cost of energy rewards buying at low prices, but peak demand charges discourage concentrating purchases in short periods. Balancing these incentives is challenging when future prices are unknown: a large purchase can establish a peak that later decisions cannot undo. We develop a peak-aware online algorithm that balances price and peak control with deadline feasibility and achieves the order-optimal competitive ratio. We further extend our results to a learning-augmented algorithm that uses predictions of optimal purchasing decisions to achieve an order-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff, exploiting accurate advice while retaining worst-case guarantees in the face of arbitrary prediction errors. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms in a case study on electricity procurement using historical electricity price traces to understand the benefits of peak-aware purchasing.

entry.title: Pipelining vs. Combining in Aggregation Tasks
entry.summary: We study the aggregation task (convergecast) in networks in the case that the values to be aggregated do not fit in a single message. We assume that every node starts with an input value, and there is an aggregation operator that is commutative, associative, and length-preserving, i.e., the result of aggregating two values has the same length as each of the input values. Since values do not fit in a message, they are transferred in a ``train'' of pipelined messages, which must be terminated whenever we want to aggregate values. The goal is to minimize the makespan time of aggregating all values. We present general lower bounds on the problem and optimal algorithms for several prevalent parallel computing architectures, including the hypercube and complete bipartite graphs, under both the splittable and unsplittable flows models. We also present an $O(\log n)$ approximation for general graphs in the unsplittable flows model.

entry.title: A Sharp Analysis of Fixed Offset Hash Tables
entry.summary: We consider the class of open addressing hash tables that uses a fixed offset sequence $r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_{n-1}$ to find an open slot in the table. As special cases this subsumes linear probing ($r_i=i$) and quadratic probing ($r_i=i^2$). We give a simple analysis that the expected insertion time when the load factor is $1-ε$ is $O(ε^{-2})$. This bound is tight for linear probing (but not for quadratic probing), so the analysis cannot be improved at this level of generality.

entry.title: Hardness and Approximation for Compressing Deterministic Finite Automata
entry.summary: The delayed deterministic finite automaton ($\text{D}^2\text{FA}$) is a powerful tool for compressing the prohibitively large deterministic finite automata (DFAs) used in modern signature-based deep packet inspection systems. A $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ augments a DFA with unlabeled default transitions to remove transitions that are similar. This technique works well in practice and has inspired numerous subsequent studies. However, existing approaches do not guarantee a $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ of optimal size as they restrict the default transitions to form a forest. In this paper, we consider the problem of finding an optimal $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$. We make the key observation that cycles of default transitions can be valid and produce a smaller $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$, provided that for every character in the alphabet, at least one state in the cycle has an outgoing transition labeled by that character. This observation raises fundamental questions concerning the computational complexity of finding an optimal $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ and the approximation guarantee of the standard (forest-restricted) approach. We answer both questions by showing that it is NP-hard to find an optimal $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ and by proving that the standard approach provides a $3/2$-approximation to the optimum. To establish NP-hardness, we construct a reduction from set cover using a DFA with gadgets where valid default transition choices correspond to selecting sets. To prove our approximation ratio, we compare the cycles in an optimal solution to a variant where the default transitions form a forest. Finally, we demonstrate that this $3/2$ ratio is tight via a constructed family of DFAs.

entry.title: Kempe Reachability with $k\geq 3$ Colors Is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-Complete on Claw-Free Graphs
entry.summary: A \emph{proper vertex coloring} assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices have distinct colors. A \emph{Kempe change} in a proper vertex coloring exchanges two colors on one component of the subgraph induced by the vertices of those colors. For a fixed palette of $k$ colors, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} asks whether two given proper vertex colorings of the same graph are connected by a sequence of Kempe changes. This problem is known to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. A graph is \emph{claw-free} if no vertex has three pairwise nonadjacent neighbors. The \emph{line graph} of a graph has one vertex for each edge, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the corresponding edges share an end. Line graphs are claw-free, and their Kempe changes correspond to \emph{edge-Kempe changes} in the original graph, which exchange two colors on one component of the subgraph formed by the edges of those colors. A claw-free graph with a proper $k$-coloring has maximum degree at most $2k-2$, whereas for $k\geq 4$ all proper $k$-colorings of a graph of maximum degree at most $k$ are connected by Kempe changes. We show that, for every fixed $k\geq 3$, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} with $k$ colors is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on line graphs of connected simple $k$-regular graphs, and hence even on connected $(2k-2)$-regular claw-free graphs. Equivalently, deciding whether two proper $k$-edge-colorings are connected by edge-Kempe changes is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on connected simple $k$-regular graphs.
