The author takes full responsibility for the correctness and content of the paper.

entry.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for $k$-Path Vertex Cover Reconfiguration on Trees under Token Sliding
entry.summary: A $k$-path vertex cover ($k$-PVC) of a graph is a set of vertices meeting every path on $k$ vertices. In Token Sliding, one token occupies each vertex of a cover; a move slides one token along an edge to an unoccupied vertex, preserving the cover property. We study whether two covers of a tree are joined by such moves. The case $k=2$ admits a linear-time decision algorithm. For every integer $k\geq2$, we give an $O(kn^2)$-time decision algorithm on trees of order $n$, with $k$ part of the input. Two covers are reachable precisely when their rigid tokens, which never move, occupy the same set and every component remaining after their deletion has the same token count. The proof transforms configurations of equal size without rigid tokens into a canonical configuration built on properly rooted subtrees, whose paths on $k$ vertices pass through their roots. A rooted-subtree recurrence identifies movable candidate tokens. We also give a direct recursive construction between the supplied endpoints, returning at most $8n^2\,3^{\lceil n/2\rceil}$ slides in $O(n^{10}3^{n/2})$ time. ChatGPT 6 Pro and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to assist with developing and reviewing mathematical arguments and drafting and revising the paper. The author takes full responsibility for the correctness and content of the paper.

entry.title: Iterative Randomized Rounding for Better-Than-2 k-Median Approximation
entry.summary: We study the classic $k$-median problem and refine the iterative rounding framework recently introduced by Byrka, Guo, Hu, Li, Wan, and Wang [FOCS'26], which yields a $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation. Our algorithm opens $k+O(1)$ facilities and achieves an expected connection cost of at most $1.9999$ times the value of the standard LP relaxation. Although the numerical improvement over $2$ is small, it establishes a conceptual result: the integrality gap of the standard relaxation is strictly below $2$ when a constant number of extra facilities is allowed. This partially answers an open question of Li and Svensson [STOC'13]. Combined with their reduction, our result yields a $1.9999$-approximation algorithm for $k$-median. Our approach builds on several technical ingredients. First, we develop a preprocessing routine that makes the LP solution $\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)$-integral, at the cost of a $(1+\varepsilon)$ factor in the connection cost and $O(1)$ extra facilities. Unlike the preprocessing of Byrka et al. [FOCS'26], our conversion is unconditional: it requires no special treatment of clients whose fractional facilities are concentrated. Next, we show that the main rounding algorithm can open facilities one at a time, eliminating the batch processing used by Byrka et al. [FOCS'26]. Finally, the improvement over 2 comes from a tighter analysis for clients whose distances from to its facilities are not all equal, and a complementary algorithm for the case in which these distances are nearly uniform.

entry.title: Almost tight distributed approximation for domination in sparse graph classes
entry.summary: We study distributed approximation of Minimum Dominating Set in a very general class of sparse graphs, extending near-optimal approximation results from the minor-free setting to bounded expansion. In more detail, for fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon>0$, we give a new deterministic constant-round LOCAL algorithm for Minimum Dominating Set on graphs of maximum average degree at most $d$ and bounded depth-one shallow-minor density. Its approximation ratio is $d+1+\varepsilon$, which is optimal up to $\varepsilon$ for every even integer $d\geq 2$. This improves on the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz by extending beyond proper minor-closed classes. From this algorithm, we derive almost-tight constant-round approximations for a number of graph classes. We get $(7+\varepsilon)$-approximations for planar graphs and graphs of bounded Euler genus, and $(5+\varepsilon)$-approximations for their triangle-free subclasses. This answers the $7+\varepsilon$ question of Wawrzyniak positively, and matches the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz. We also apply our algorithm to classes of bounded queue-number or stack-number, obtaining bounds that are tight up to $\varepsilon$. Additionally, we answer questions of Amiri and Siebertz about improving the dependence of the round complexity on $1/\varepsilon$ and obtaining polynomial local computation for fixed parameters, when comparing the output to the usual domination number.

entry.title: Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum: Subexponential Algorithm, Tight Lower Bounds, and Average-Case Analysis
entry.summary: The Equal Subset Sum problem asks, given n positive integers bounded by M, to find two distinct non-empty subsets with the same sum. We study this problem in the regime $M = 2^{o(n)}$, where the pigeonhole principle guarantees that a solution exists, and the main challenge is to find one efficiently. A straightforward dynamic-programming algorithm runs in time poly(n).$M$. After a sequence of improvements, the current best algorithm, due to Jin, Williams, and Zhang (ESA 2025), achieves running time poly(n).$M^{1/3}$. In this work, we give the first poly(n).$M^{o(1)}$-time algorithm for Equal Subset Sum in the regime $M = 2^{o(n)}$. We complement this algorithmic result with a tight conditional lower bound showing that any substantial improvement would require a major breakthrough in approximation algorithms for lattice problems, building on recent techniques of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan (STOC 2025). Finally, we show that our techniques yield an asymptotically faster algorithm for the regime when $M = Θ(2^{n})$: a poly(n)$\cdot 2^{n/4}$-time algorithm in the average case.

entry.title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
entry.summary: Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering. Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.

entry.title: Near-Quadratic Time Multivariate Polynomial Interpolation
entry.summary: Let $\F$ be a finite field. Given $N$ distinct points $\bmα_1,\ldots,\bmα_N \in \F^m$ and associated values $β_1,\ldots,β_N \in \F$, we study the problem of computing an $m$-variate polynomial $f(\vy) \in \F[\vy]$ of individual degree less than $d$, with $d^m \ge N$, that satisfies $f(\bmα_i)=β_i$ for all $i\in[N]$, whenever such an $f$ exists. This is known as the\textit{ multivariate polynomial interpolation} problem. In this work, given $N=d^m$, we present a deterministic algorithm for multivariate polynomial interpolation over an arbitrary finite field $\F$ that runs in near-quadratic time $N^{2+o(1)}\poly(m,d,\log|\F|)$, assuming $d$ is $ω(1)$. This bound holds whenever the associated \emph{multivariate Vandermonde} matrix is nonsingular, has constant co-rank, or admits some special structure. In the general case, we give a randomized Las Vegas algorithm attaining the same near-quadratic running time, provided the finite field is sufficiently large and $d$ grows similar to the previous case. Unlike other multivariate interpolation strategies, we do not assume black-box access to the polynomial. In particular, we are not permitted to query arbitrary input points to obtain their evaluations. Our interpolation result follows by combining Wiedemann's classical approach~\cite{w86} for solving sparse linear systems with known bounds for fast \emph{multivariate multipoint evaluation} over finite fields~\cite{umans08, KU11, BGKM23, BGGKU24}. Specifically, our deterministic interpolation strategy relies on a deterministic variant of Wiedemann's approach, which is more commonly used in the randomized setting.

entry.title: Report the tolerance, not the count: exact phylogenetic distance deconvolution with incomplete references
entry.summary: Phylogenetic distance deconvolution represents mixture-to-reference distances by weighted sources placed on a reference tree. We study the minimum number of strictly interior sources that explains a distance profile, and what incomplete references cost. On a positive-rational reduced tree we give an exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves; the single-exponential dependence on K is tight under ETH, already with every leaf observed. With arbitrary missing references and a prescribed pendant the problem is W[1]-hard in the source budget K, even on positive binary trees supplied with a strict explanation using at most K+1 sources. We then use the algorithm as an instrument. Removing references can only lower the minimum source count, never raise it, at every error tolerance. Which references are missing then matters far more than how many. Under nearest-to-source deletion a median of two references can be erased before the generating support stops being the unique smallest explanation, and that budget stays nearly flat as the panel grows (Spearman 0.10 over 20 to 361 references, against 0.82 for random loss). Discarding 7,931 of 10,575 references from a real 16S panel at random costs 1.8% of the tolerance at which one source suffices. Discarding comparably many as whole clades costs 90%. That tolerance needs neither ground truth nor an error model, which makes the model measurable on real data. The generating configuration's worst-leaf residual exceeds the one-source optimum in all 296 real ANI cases, and in 248 after refitting the common pendant. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice. A point estimate of the count alone does not quantify it. Methods for this problem should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.

entry.title: Optimal Mixing for Local Edge-Coloring Dynamics on Trees
entry.summary: We study the mixing time of two local Markov chains for uniformly sampling proper edge colorings of trees. For a tree with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $Δ$, we establish optimal mixing-time bounds for the single-edge Glauber dynamics when $q\geΔ+2$ and for the neighboring-edge heat-bath dynamics when $q\geΔ+1$. Both chains mix in $O_Δ(n(\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)))$ steps, uniformly over the number of colors $q$. These bounds are tight in their dependence on $n$ for fixed $Δ$. Our proof establishes log-Sobolev inequalities through local color release, reusable recoloring buffers, and component entropy mixing. The two dynamics require different local constructions: a two-spare-color buffer for single-edge updates and a second-layer controller for neighboring-edge updates. The resulting entropy analysis applies to general bounded-degree trees, including regimes where worst-case spatial mixing fails.

entry.title: The Cost of Missed States: Online Tracking with Current-Observation Resets
entry.summary: An online tracker retains one state and may reset only to the current observation, although its complete observed history is available. Offline knows the future and obeys the same reset rule. Under a hard discrepancy radius, for every horizon $T\ge5$ and every feasible randomized causal policy, a fixed path on a known five-point metric requires at least $(T+1)/2$ expected refreshes, against exactly two offline refreshes with a strict radius margin. Missing the useful prefix center forces a refresh at every suffix observation. The path visits four values, with resolution fixed as $T$ grows. Write $J_λ$ for cumulative discrepancy plus a charge $λ>0$ per refresh, and $V_T$ for the sum of successive observation distances. A candidate prefix adapts Bienkowski and Schmid's randomized lower bound to this objective under current resets, even with a known horizon and $V_T<3λ$. This construction needs finer grids; a fixed finite metric with positive minimum separation instead admits a competitive policy for penalized tracking. An anytime policy satisfies $J_λ\leλ+4\sqrt{λTV_T}$ without knowing the horizon or final variation. Clipping for a known horizon gives $J_λ\leλT$ and a factor-three comparison with the minimum of three analytical bounds, without knowing final variation. Current-value diameter and readout sensitivity give same-input output bounds for mixtures, including squared-distance softmax.

entry.title: Polynomial pathwidth for graphs vertex-coverable by few shortest paths and algorithms for quasi-shortest path covers
entry.summary: We study how covering a graph by a small number of shortest or approximately shortest paths/walks constrains its treewidth and pathwidth. A path or walk is $(α,β)$-quasi-shortest for $α\geq1$ and $β\geq 0$ if each contiguous segment has length at most $α$ times the distance between its endpoints plus $β$. For graphs vertex-covered by $k$ shortest paths, we establish the first known polynomial pathwidth bound of $O(k^3)$. For edge-coverage, we improve the previously known $O(k^4)$ upper bound to $O(k^2\log k)$. As a main ingredient of the proofs, we first show that if the vertices of a graph can be covered by $k$ $(α,β)$-quasi-shortest paths or walks, then its treewidth is $O_{α,β}(k^2)$; this is a consequence of the fact that such graphs have linear metric growth and the technique developed in [Campbell et al., E-JC 2023]. To obtain the above pathwidth upper bounds, we combine this result with techniques from the literature in a nontrivial way. On the other hand, we show that there exist connected bipartite cubic graph whose edges can be covered by $k$ shortest paths and whose pathwidth is $Ω(k\log k)$, providing the first superlinear lower bound. For graphs covered by $k=2$ $(α,0)$-quasi-shortest paths with $α>1$, we show that, unlike treewidth and unlike the case $α=1$ and $β=0$ of exact shortest paths, the pathwidth may be unbounded. Finally, for every fixed rationals $α\geq1$ and $β\geq 0$, we give XP algorithms with a running time of $n^{f(k,α,β)}$ for some function~$f$ that decide whether the vertices of a graph can be covered by at most $k$ $(α,β)$-quasi-shortest paths or walks. The algorithms combine our treewidth upper bounds with an algorithmic meta-theorem from [Dreier et al., LICS 2025]. [abstract shortened to meet the arXiv requirements]

entry.title: Tight Bounds for Paging with Time Windows and Joint Replenishment with Varying Opening Costs
entry.summary: We study the paging with time windows problem, a natural generalization of classical paging, in which each request must be served within a specified time interval. This model allows the algorithm to delay service and batch service requests over time, but also introduces significant challenges due to overlapping requests. While the problem is well understood in the unweighted setting, where optimal $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithms are known, the weighted case remains more elusive. The best previously known algorithm, due to Gupta, Kumar, and Panigrahi, achieves an $O(\log k \log n)$-competitive ratio, leaving a gap between weighted and unweighted settings. We obtain an $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithm for weighted paging with time windows, matching the optimal competitive ratio. The core of our approach is a structural decomposition that separates the evolution of the cache from the scheduling of page loads. We show that, given a sequence of cache configurations, computing a near-optimal sequence of page loads reduces to a variant of the Joint Replenishment Problem with deadlines (JRP-D) with time-dependent opening costs. We design a constant-competitive online algorithm for this variant and prove that the reduction is tight. Combining this with an existing online construction of cache configurations yields the desired bound.

entry.title: Temporal Exploration and Rendezvous via Weisfeiler-Leman Colorings
entry.summary: Temporal graphs are graphs whose edge relation changes in discrete time steps. The Temporal Exploration Problem (TEXP) asks for a temporal walk that visits all vertices. We show that every connected temporal graph with $n$ vertices can be explored in $O(qn\log^3(n))$ time steps, where $q$ is the number of vertex color classes induced by the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (2-WL) coloring. For small $q$, our bound substantially improves on the known worst-case bound of $Θ(n^2)$ in general connected temporal graphs. A corresponding walk can be constructed in deterministic polynomial time. The upper bound is complemented by lower bounds of $Ω(n\log(n))$ when $q$ is constant and $Ω(qn)$ when $1 \leq q \leq n$. We also apply our techniques to the Temporal Rendezvous Problem (TRP), in which two agents that do not communicate have to meet on a vertex of the temporal graph. Our exploration algorithm yields that, with only polynomial-time computational power, the agents can meet in $O(n\log^3(n))$ time steps, leaving a gap of only $\log^2(n)$ to the known lower bound. Dogeas, Erlebach, Kammer, Meintrup, and Moses Jr. [ICALP'24] have shown an $O(rn^{1+ε})$ bound for TEXP, for every fixed $ε> 0$, where $r$ is the number of orbits, and an $O(n^{1+ε})$ bound for TRP. Both results require superpolynomial computation time. Our contribution improves upon these results in several ways. First, the dependence on $n$ in the upper bounds on the number of time steps is decreased from $n^{1+ε}$ to $n\log^3(n)$ for both TEXP and TRP. Second, for TEXP, we bound the number of time steps linearly by the parameter q, which is efficiently computable and upper bounded by $r$. Third, we provide novel deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for both TEXP and TRP.

entry.title: Approximation and Inapproximability of Non-Preemptive Dial-a-Ride
entry.summary: The non-preemptive dial-a-ride problem (DaRP) asks for a minimum-cost route of a capacitated vehicle that serves a collection of pickup-and-delivery requests, without allowing objects to be transferred or temporarily unloaded. We study this problem and the closely related minimum-ratio Steiner $k$-Forest (S$k$F) in general symmetric metrics on $n$ locations. We develop a randomized polynomial-time algorithm with expected approximation ratio $\mathcal{O}(n^{1/4}\log^{11}n)$ for the minimum-ratio S$k$F. Our algorithm combines a deterministic approximation on hierarchically well-separated trees with randomized metric embeddings. Using this algorithm, we obtain expected $\mathcal{O}(n^{1/4}\log^{12}n)$-approximations for both the non-preemptive DaRP and the S$k$F. These guarantees improve on the previous $n^{0.3+\varepsilon}$-approximation ratios for the S$k$F and the non-preemptive DaRP, where $\varepsilon>0$ is any fixed constant. Complementing these algorithmic results, we establish the first superconstant inapproximability bounds for the non-preemptive DaRP. Under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm achieves an $x^{1/(\log\log x)^c}$-approximation for some constant $c>0$, where $x$ denotes either the number of locations $n$ or the vehicle capacity $k$. Under the quantitative Gap-ETH, we rule out every deterministic polynomial-time $x^{o(1)}$-approximation. These bounds hold even on unit-edge stars with $n=(2+o(1))k$.

entry.title: Pre-emptive Carbon Aware Scheduling for Edge Workloads
entry.summary: Power grids use a constantly changing mix of fossil fuels and clean renewables like solar and wind. Because of this, the {\em carbon footprint} fluctuates drastically based on time and geographic location. Time-varying carbon intensity creates opportunities to reduce carbon emissions by shifting workloads to cleaner periods, but deadlines, task dependencies, and limited edge capacity constrain this flexibility. We study carbon-aware scheduling of jobs with release times, deadlines, and arbitrary precedence constraints under piecewise-constant carbon costs. Jobs execute preemptively on a single edge server or are outsourced at job-dependent costs to an unlimited-capacity cloud, modeled as providing instantaneous execution. The objective is to minimize the sum of edge carbon costs and cloud outsourcing costs while satisfying all timing and precedence constraints. For edge-only execution, we give an exact polynomial-time algorithm. Allowing cloud outsourcing makes the problem NP-hard, but we obtain a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme through a reduction to preemptive scheduling with rejection penalties (weighted tardiness). In contrast, even two edge servers without job migration admit no polynomially bounded approximation when carbon-cost variation is unrestricted, unless \(P=NP\). We complement these theoretical results with experiments on controlled synthetic workloads and production-derived Alibaba traces. On synthetic instances, our incremental max-flow implementation is $4.96\times$ faster on average than a direct min-cost flow, while experiements on production-derived workloads evaluate its performance under realistic job structures.

entry.title: A Sharp Dynamic Haussler Lemma
entry.summary: Haussler's covering lemma (JCTA 1995) gives the sharp $(C/δ)^d$ metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes under normalized $\ell_1$ distance. We prove a sharp global dynamic analogue for bounded real-valued classes in normalized $\ell_p$, for every $1\le p<\infty$. Writing $d=\operatorname{sfat}_{\varepsilon/32}(\mathcal F)$, we obtain a global dynamic cover of size at most $(C/\varepsilon^p)^d$ for every horizon and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Here a single family of deterministic causal experts, fixed independently of the instance sequence, covers every target on every sequence. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, a matching worst-case lower bound $(c/\varepsilon)^{pd}$ holds already for binary classes on one fixed sequence, even with real-valued experts. The constants are universal, independent of $p$. For $p=2$, this resolves the horizon-independent sequential $\ell_2$ covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (PTRF 2015) in a stronger global form. For $p=1$, it gives the sharp $(C/δ)^{\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal H)}$ global dynamic covering bound for binary classes, resolving questions of Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Dagan, Moran, Naor, and Yogev (STOC 2021) and Malliaris and Moran (Trans. AMS 2024). Our proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules and accurate sampled prefixes with exact continuations after target identification. Shared-parent routing distributes these continuations among eligible prefixes, eliminating the logarithmic overhead.

entry.title: Asymmetric Likelihood-Free Hypothesis Testing
entry.summary: In likelihood-free hypothesis testing (LFHT), given samples from two unknown distributions $P,Q$ on $[n]$ with $\mathrm{d_{TV}}(P,Q)\geq\varepsilon$, and from a third distribution $D\in\{P,Q\}$, the goal is to identify whether $D=P$ or $D=Q$. We study asymmetric likelihood-free hypothesis testing, where the sample budgets $s_P$ and $s_Q$ for $P$ and $Q$ may differ, and characterize the feasible triples $(s_P,s_Q,s_D)$ up to logarithmic factors. We establish that unequal reference budgets can give a polynomial saving. For instance, for constant separation, $n$ samples from $P$ and $n^{3/4}$ from $Q$ allow testing with $\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$ samples from $D$, whereas both existing baselines---symmetric LFHT and unequal-sample closeness testing---require $Ω(\sqrt n)$ samples from $D$. We further apply our results to non-adaptive distribution 2-clustering, where the sample allocation among $k$ distributions must be fixed before observing any data. We obtain matching upper and lower bounds for this problem up to logarithmic factors in terms of the domain size, number of distributions, smaller cluster size, and separation, both with one cluster distribution known and with both unknown. Comparing with known bounds for adaptive sample allocation gives a worst-case adaptivity gap of $\widetildeΘ(k^{1/4})$.

entry.title: An experimental evaluation of static k-center clustering algorithms on graphs
entry.summary: The $k$-center problem is one of the most fundamental clustering problems and has applications in a wide range of areas, including facility location, network design, data mining, and machine learning. Given a set of objects together with a distance measure, the goal is to select $k$ centers such that the maximum distance from any object to its closest center is minimized. The $k$-center problem has been studied extensively from a theoretical perspective, both in metric spaces and on graphs. While there have been experimental studies for $k$-center clustering in metric spaces, a comprehensive experimental comparison of graph-based $k$-center algorithms on large-scale graphs is still lacking. In this paper, we bridge this gap by evaluating a set of algorithms ranging from classical approaches such as Gonzalez's greedy algorithm [TCS 1985], an algorithm based on the framework established by Hochbaum and Shmoys [Math. Oper. Res. 1985], to more recent methods, including algorithms by Thorup [SICOMP 2001] and Abboud et al. [SOSA 2023]. Our study considers both running time, solution quality and the effects of parallelism on a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art $k$-center algorithms on graphs and identify the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches in practice.

entry.title: Fully Dynamic Triangle and 4-Vertex Subgraph Counting: From Theory to Practice and Back Again
entry.summary: Counting small patterns is a core primitive in large-scale graph analytics, with numerous applications in data management and network analysis. As modern graphs are massive and continuously evolving, maintaining such counts efficiently under updates is essential. Although specialized dynamic algorithms for patterns with up to four vertices exist, they remain largely theoretical; practitioners instead rely on general-purpose or approximate methods. We present an in-depth study of two dynamic approaches by Eppstein et al. and Hanauer et al. for maintaining counts of triangles and all connected four-vertex subgraph patterns, both based on variants of heavy-light vertex partitioning. We introduce theoretical and practical optimizations and develop hybrid variants that combine complementary strengths of both approaches. Experiments on 56 large real-world and synthetic dynamic graphs show that our optimized algorithms outperform the original methods and strong static and dynamic baselines on nearly all instances, both in total running time and worst-case update time, with speedups of up to several orders of magnitude. We further provide practical guidelines for algorithm selection and tuning. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive empirical study of heavy-light partitioning for dynamic subgraph counting, and our findings may inform other algorithms based on this technique.

entry.title: A Tight Space Lower Bound for Pivot-Based Distance Oracles
entry.summary: An approximate distance oracle (ADO) is a compact data structure that answers distance queries within a multiplicative \emph{stretch} $k$. The classical oracle of Thorup and Zwick~[STOC'01, JACM'05] has stretch $k=2\ell-1$ and uses $O(\ell n^{1+1/\ell})$ space, for every integer $\ell\ge1$, and this trade-off is optimal for dense graphs under the Erdős girth conjecture. However, for sparse graphs ($m=O(n)$), their lower bound yields nothing beyond $Ω(m)$ space. A pivot-based $1$-hop ADO gives every vertex $\tilde{O}(1)$ pivots and returns as an estimate the length of a walk of the form $u\to p_u \to p_v \to v$, where $p_u$ is a pivot of $u$, $p_v$ is a pivot of $v$, and $p_u\to p_v$ is a stored distance. We observe that all the state-of-the-art ADOs with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time are in fact pivot-based $1$-hop ADOs. Our main result is that, under the Erdős girth conjecture for graphs with constant degree, there are sparse graphs on which every \emph{pivot-based} $1$-hop ADO with stretch $k$ requires $\widetildeΩ(m^{1+2/(k+1)})$ space, for every \emph{real} $k\ge1$. This matches the best known upper bounds with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time, up to polylogarithmic factors, at every stretch where they are known. We also extend our lower bound to pivot-based ADOs with any constant number $β$ of hops, showing that they require $\widetildeΩ(m^{1+2/(β(k+1))})$ space. In addition, we obtain a tight lower bound for two-hop hopsets. Under the Erdős girth conjecture, for every integer $\ell\ge3$, $(2\ell-3,2)$-hopsets on sparse graphs require size $Ω(m^{1+1/\ell})$, which matches a construction based on the oracles of [Kadria and Roditty, ISAAC'25]. Using the recent explicit high-girth graphs of Double Agent~[doubleAI'26], we also obtain unconditional versions of our ADO lower bounds, with the exponent above $1$ multiplied by $4/5$.

entry.title: Dynamically optimal weight-balanced binary search trees
entry.summary: In STOC 1972, J{ü}rg Nievergelt and Edward M.~Reingold introduced the $BB[α]$-tree, also known as a \emph{weight-balanced} tree, which for any $α\in (0,\frac{1}{2}]$ is a binary search tree where every node with induced subtree size $s$ has children with induced subtree sizes at least $α(s+1)-1$. A new rotation-based binary search tree, the \emph{PopTree}, is introduced. The PopTree stores $n$ elements and is a $BB[\tfrac1{20}]$-tree after the execution of each search and a $BB[\tfrac1{729}]$-tree at all times, notably while rebalancing. For any constant $α$, its performance on search sequences of length $Ω(n \log n)$ is proved to be within a constant factor (which can depend on $α$) of the optimal offline rotation-based binary search tree that maintains the $BB[α]$ balance invariant.

entry.title: How to Walk a Dog in Parallel: On Parallel Computation of the Discrete Frechet Distance
entry.summary: The Fréchet distance (also known as the dog-leash distance) is a well-studied and prevalent distance measure for polygonal curves. In this paper we present parallel algorithms for computing the discrete \frechet\ distance between two curves, in both the PRAM and MPC models. For two polygonal curves of length $n$, we show that the distance between them can be computed in the PRAM model in $O(\log n/ σ)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{2+σ})$ total work for any $0<σ<1$. In the sublinear MPC model with $n^ρ$ space per machine, it can be computed in $O(\log n / ρ^2)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{2+ρ})$ total space. For $c$-packed curves, we match our bounds to the sequential algorithms, showing that a $(1+\eps)$-approximation of the distance can be computed in the PRAM model in $O(\log{n}+1/σ^3)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{1+σ})$ total work, and in the sublinear MPC model in $O(1 /ρ^3)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{1+ρ})$ total space, for any constant $\eps>0$. As part of our algorithms for $c$-packed curves, we also present parallel algorithms for computing curve simplifications, which may be of independent interest.

entry.title: On the Largest Cardinality Subset Sum
entry.summary: We study Largest Cardinality Subset Sum (LCSS): given $n$ nonnegative integers and a target $t$, compute a subset summing to $t$ with maximum cardinality. We also consider its all-targets version (ATLCSS), which asks for this maximum for every sum $s\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$. The LCSS problem sits squarely between the subset sum and the knapsack problem. A straightforward dynamic-programming algorithm runs in time $O(nt)$ and solves ATLCSS, and using Jin and Bringmann (both in STOC 2024, independent work) $0$-$1$ knapsack results we achieve a $\widetilde{O}(n + a_{\max}^2)$-time deterministic algorithm for LCSS. Our main result is a randomized $\widetilde{O}(n+\sqrt{n}\,t)$-time algorithm for LCSS. Then, we complement this result with a randomized $\widetilde{O}(n+t^{3/2})$-time algorithm for ATLCSS. Together, our two algorithms give a $\widetilde{O}(n+t\min\{\sqrt{n},\sqrt{t}\})$-time algorithm for LCSS. As an application of ATLCSS, we solve the search version of Projection Subset Sum, introduced by Dutta and Rajasree (SYNSAC 2023), in $\widetilde{O}(n+t^{3/2})$ time for every fixed $\ell_p$ norm with $p\geq 1$. For $\ell_1$, we obtain $\widetilde{O}(n+t)$ time, removing the unique-representation assumption required by their algorithm. Both algorithms output an optimal modified vector and a witnessing subset.

entry.title: Optimal Labeling Schemes for $Γ$-Free Matrices
entry.summary: We study labeling schemes for $p \times q$ $Γ$-free binary matrices, which do not contain a submatrix of the form $Γ= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. We give a labeling scheme that uses $O(\log^2 N)$-bit labels for rows and columns, where $N=p+q$, such that any matrix entry can be determined from the corresponding two labels in constant time in the word RAM model. The worst-case label size matches the counting lower bound up to constant factors. We also show that the entrywise least $Γ$-free supermatrix of an arbitrary $p\times q$ binary matrix, together with its labels, can be constructed in $O(pq)$ time. Our construction represents a $Γ$-free matrix by a sequence of rooted forests, where each column corresponds to a node and the $1$-entries of each row form a root path in its corresponding forest. For $n$-vertex strongly chordal and chordal bipartite graphs, our result gives asymptotically optimal $O(\log^2 n)$-bit adjacency labeling schemes with constant-time queries. These results answer both representation questions posed by Spinrad in 1995.

entry.title: Near-Optimal Consistency-Robustness Bounds for Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling
entry.summary: We study the problem of characterizing the optimal consistency--robustness tradeoff for single-machine non-clairvoyant scheduling with predicted processing times. For a fixed number of jobs $n$, Wei and Zhang (2020) established a lower bound on the achievable consistency--robustness tradeoff which is known to be tight only in a few restrictive cases, leaving the optimal tradeoff for general $n$ unresolved. A different worst-case-$n$ regime was introduced by Benomar et al. (2025), who applied the former work's construction to show that for $λ\in (0, 1)$, any $(1+λ)$-consistent algorithm must be $1 + Ω(\sqrt{1/λ})$-robust. On the other hand, the best known upper bound gives $(1+λ)$-consistency and $1+O(1/λ)$-robustness, leaving a polynomial gap. In this work, we develop a new lower bound using a multi-stage adversarial construction and a new algorithm that together give a near-optimal characterization of the consistency--robustness tradeoff: for every $n$, our upper bound is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of our lower bound, and thus our algorithm is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of the online optimal. In particular, our lower bound shows that any $(1+λ)$-consistent algorithm must have robustness at least $1/\sqrtλ$ as $n \to \infty$, while our algorithm achieves robustness at most $\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}+1/λ}$ for any $n$, matching the lower bound in the leading term as $λ\downarrow 0$; our upper bound also closes the polynomial gap in the worst-case-$n$ regime. We additionally show how our algorithm can be made error-tolerant, preserving the near-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff while incurring only slightly degraded performance under bounded prediction errors.

entry.title: The Optimal Sampler for Diverse TSP Solutions: Characterization, Limits, and Learning
entry.summary: We address the Diverse Traveling Salesman Problem (D-TSP) that seeks a set of $k$ distinct TSP tours. Each selected tour must not exceed a prescribed multiple of the optimal tour length, while the maximum pairwise Jaccard similarity within the selected set is minimized. This formulation is important for applications requiring both solution quality and fault tolerance, such as logistics planning, robotics, and strategic patrolling. We propose a novel hybrid framework that decomposes D-TSP into a sampling stage and a selection stage. The selection stage is a max-min dispersion problem, for which any approximation better than a factor of two is NP-hard; we therefore focus on the sampling stage. Our contributions are both theoretical and empirical. Theoretically, we give two end-to-end guarantees for the optimal sampling distribution, from two perspectives: including an optimal set in the sampled pool, or having at least $k$ mutually distant tours in the pool. The second reduces the number of samples from exponential to linear in $k$, at the cost of weakening the benchmark from the best $k$ tours to the best $βk$ for some $β> 1$. For practical use, we prove that a pipeline that samples spanning trees and then converts to tours does not hurt the quality of the pool in principle. Empirically, both objectives are learnable, and our experiments not only validate the analysis but also outperform the baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, by a single trained model with no fine-tuning.

entry.title: Solving problems in RDV Graphs faster and easier
entry.summary: In interval graphs and many generalizations thereof, problems such as Matching, Independent Set, and Dominating Set can be solved with simple greedy algorithms in linear (i.e., $O(m+n)$) time. However, it is sometimes possible to improve on this runtime if a suitable representation as intersection graph is given; for example it is possible to find a minimum dominating set in an interval graph in $O(n)$ time. We study RDV graphs, a generalization of interval graphs, namely, the intersection graphs of directed paths in a rooted tree. It was known that the above three problems can be solved in $O(n\log n)$ time if a suitably small representation is given. In this paper, we reduce the runtime to $O(n)$. Furthermore, while the previous results used non-trivial operations such as range-minimum queries and ray-shooting queries, we need nothing more complicated than lists and (for Matching) a Union-Find data structure.

entry.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
entry.summary: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $[N]$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted and collision detection is unavailable. Our neighborhood-clearing procedure reuses an elected receiver to secure its entire closed in-neighborhood in $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. Charging each distinct closed neighborhood once yields $\mathcal O(m\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds under an explicit degree-concentration condition, for every polynomial identifier range. A complementary adaptive-pruning procedure combines quadratic contraction with completion sensitive to the number of unsecured sources. If $a\ge1$ sources remain at completion entry, permutation selectors reduce the balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. A geometric execution attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+nτ+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for a path cover of scale $k$, weight $τ$, and $u$ exceptions. For directed graphs with common in- and out-degree $Δ$, the portfolio achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrtΔ,n^2/Δ\})$. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs; degrees, covers, and structural constants are used solely in the analysis. The unrestricted polynomial-identifier density extension remains open.

entry.title: Birthday Estimators Are Uniformly Optimal for Renyi Entropy
entry.summary: Collisions are a basic probe of unknown distributions, used for testing and for counting substructures in graphs, and they underlie Rényi entropy, a fundamental measure of uncertainty with applications in cryptography, machine learning, physics, and biology. Motivated by this, we study the natural birthday estimator. We prove Bernstein-type concentration for it and show that it is minimax optimal, uniformly and jointly in alphabet size, order, accuracy, and confidence, with no sample splitting, clipping, or median aggregation. This, in particular, settles the sample complexity of integer-order Rényi entropy estimation up to absolute constants in all regimes, closing the gap between the best known upper and lower bounds. Our concentration bound rests on a sensitivity analysis of collision count, and the matching lower bound on a sharp analysis of detecting a hidden spike in a plateau distribution.

entry.title: Dynamic Distances Without Matrix Inverse
entry.summary: We study the fully dynamic exact distance problem in unweighted directed graphs, where the graph undergoes edge insertions and deletions, and the distance between two query vertices must be reported. Under the combinatorial Boolean matrix multiplication conjecture, any subquadratic-time algorithm for this problem must use algebraic techniques. All prior work uses the polynomial matrix inverse as its algebraic tool, but within subquadratic time, this technique can only maintain distances up to a small-polynomial hop bound. So larger distances must be reassembled from short-range pieces by a combinatorial layer. This hybrid algebraic-combinatorial construction has led to a substantial slowdown for dynamic distances compared to other dynamic graph problems relying on algebraic techniques. We give the first subquadratic-time dynamic distance algorithm built on dynamically maintaining a different algebraic object than the matrix inverse. By maintaining the Frobenius form $A=KCK^{-1}$ of a dynamic generic (i.e., cyclic) matrix $A$, we can query all the powers $A^\ell = K C^\ell K^{-1}$ efficiently. For adjacency matrix~$A$, the smallest $\ell$ with $(A^\ell)_{s,t}\neq 0$ is the $st$-distance in the associated graph. So, unlike dynamic matrix inverse, we get distance information directly without hop truncation, and we no longer need to perform any combinatorial reassembly. This purely algebraic approach to dynamic distances leads to the fastest dynamic distance algorithm with $O(n^{1.58})$ update time. The earlier use of the Frobenius form maintained the dense change of basis $K$ explicitly and required $\tilde O (n^2)$ time per update [KS23]. Our key observation is that this change of basis is highly structured, which lets us maintain it implicitly. This gives the first subquadratic dynamic algorithm for the Frobenius normal form and characteristic polynomial for generic matrices.

entry.title: Diverse Schedules for Makespan Minimization on Unrelated Machines
entry.summary: We study makespan minimization on unrelated machines with the additional goal of constructing diverse schedules: Instead of outputting a single schedule, we seek a collection of schedules with provable makespan guarantees and substantially different job assignments. Committing to a single schedule in advance may be undesirable. Processing times may be uncertain, and constraints or domain knowledge may emerge later, so $k$ schedules of similar quality offer meaningful alternatives. We measure pairwise diversity by the weighted Hamming distance between job assignments and study the two standard objectives in the diverse-solutions literature: max-sum diversity, which maximizes the total pairwise distance between schedules, and max-min diversity, which maximizes the smallest pairwise distance. For the max-sum objective, we show that optimal diversity can be achieved in polynomial time without sacrificing the classic makespan approximation factor. For every feasible makespan target $T$, we can compute $k$ schedules of makespan at most $2T$ whose max-sum diversity is optimal among all $k$ schedules of makespan at most $T$. Therefore, we match the classic factor-$2$ makespan guarantee of Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (Math. Prog., 1990) and preserve optimal diversity. For the max-min objective, we show that the diversity problem is inherently harder. Namely, we show that, even without makespan constraints, deciding whether three schedules of given pairwise diversity exist is NP-hard. We complete this with two complementary bicriteria approximation algorithms for every fixed $k$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. The first preserves almost all of the optimal max-min diversity with makespan at most $(3\lceil12/\varepsilon\rceil+1)T$. The second keeps the makespan arbitrarily close to the classic $2$ guarantee while achieving a $\frac{1}{2}(1-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the optimal max-min diversity.

entry.title: Improved Approximation for Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Using Quota Trees
entry.summary: In the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (UCVRP), we are given a set $V$ of $n$ clients with normalized demands $d_v \in (0,1]$, a depot $r$, a unit vehicle capacity, and symmetric metric travel costs $c$ on $V \cup \{r\}$. We seek a collection of routes of minimum total cost that start and end at $r$, serve each client's entire demand on a single route, and respect the unit capacity constraint $\sum_{v \in V(R)} d_v \le 1$ on every route $R$, where $V(R)$ denotes the clients served by $R$. This models deliveries from a common depot in which each customer's order must be delivered in a single trip. UCVRP generalizes the metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) and is therefore NP-hard. Capacity constraints add a packing difficulty: when all clients are colocated away from the depot, minimizing the route cost is equivalent to minimizing the number of bins in bin packing. Consequently, UCVRP admits no polynomial-time approximation ratio below $3/2$ unless $\textbf{P=NP}$ (Grandoni, Mathieu, and Zhou, 2023). The classical $3.5$-approximation has been improved through several recent advances; in particular, Zhao and Xiao (2026) recently obtained a $(2+\ln 2+\varepsilon)$-approximation. In this paper, we give a deterministic $(5/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in $n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ time for every rational $0<\varepsilon\le1/9$, applicable to general capacity and arbitrary positive demands. Our algorithm uses local search to select routes through one client with large demand and clients with small demands. It constructs candidate routes using endpoint quota trees after rounding demands and creating vertex copies. We combine these routes with those obtained by matching and set packing, keeping their client sets disjoint. The remaining clients are served by partitioning a tour constructed using weighted graphic matroid parity.

entry.title: ARRIVAL in cube-root subexponential time
entry.summary: In the ARRIVAL problem, a token travels through a switch digraph: at every vertex, it leaves along one of two out-arcs, and the two are used alternately. The question is which of two terminals the token reaches first. ARRIVAL lies in $\mathsf{NP} \cap \mathsf{coNP}$, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known.The fastest known algorithms turn some vertices into terminals and search for consistent guesses of the numbers of tokens that these vertices send out. The first, due to Gärtner et al. [ICALP 2021], searches all vertices at once with an algorithm for fixed points of monotone maps, and the second, due to Haslebacher [ICALP 2025], searches one vertex at a time by binary search. Both search for a fixed point of the same map, which returns how many tokens arrive at the guessed vertices. We guess the vertices in blocks of $k$, between these two extremes, which needs a search in $k$ dimensions with few evaluations of this map. To do so, we build on the connection between ARRIVAL and $\ell_1$-contractions established in the second of these works. We search with $\ell_1$-centerpoints of the remaining guesses, which are guaranteed to exist by Haslebacher et al. [FOCS 2025], and which we approximate deterministically. In order to prove our results, we show how to find the least fixed points of maps from $\{0, \ldots, N\}^k$ to itself that have unit increments. For ARRIVAL on $n$-vertex switch digraphs, this gives run time $2^{\mathcal{O}(n^{1/3} \cdot \log^{2/3} n)}$, improving the previous time bound of $n^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})}$. We work with the more general \garrival problem, with many tokens and several terminals, and solve it in the same time when there are at most $2^n$ tokens.

entry.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
entry.summary: We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we: (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant; (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.

entry.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
entry.summary: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.

entry.title: Splitting Planar Necklaces with Few Straight Cuts
entry.summary: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the same number of beads of each color. We study the planar analog in which a cut is a full straight line and the objective is minimizing the number of lines: $m$ points colored red and blue must be separated by straight-line cuts into regions that can be allocated to $k$ agents so that each agent receives the same number of points of each color. Projection to a line gives $2(k-1)$ cuts, and $k-1$ are sometimes necessary; we give algorithms, static and dynamic, that provably close part of this gap. We develop several approaches that capitalize on the extra degree of freedom: a ``star'' search that produces solutions with as few as $\lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ cuts and never more than $k$ whenever a fair contiguous circular partition exists, with further guarantees for evenly spaced input, and a general algorithm that produces at most $k + \log_2(k+1) - 2$ cuts in $Θ(m \log k)$ time, built on a one-dimensional necklace splitting subroutine that requires no presorting. We then adapt the general algorithm to a dynamic setting, maintaining exact fairness and the cut bound under arbitrary relocation of points, with expected update time that scales with the total distance moved.

entry.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Results for the Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set Problem
entry.summary: We study the \emph{Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set} problem (MEG-Set), which asks for a minimum-cardinality set $M$ of vertices of an undirected graph $G$ of $n$ vertices such that every edge of $G$ belongs to all shortest paths between some pair of vertices in $M$. We present new approximation and hardness results for MEG-Set. On the positive side, we design a deterministic polynomial-time $O(n^{1/3}\log^{2/3}n)$-approximation algorithm, improving upon the previously best-known $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ approximation ratio. On the negative side, for every constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we prove that the problem admits no polynomial-time $\big(2^{\log^{1-\varepsilon} n}\big)$-approximation algorithm, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq \mathsf{DTIME}(n^{\operatorname{polylog} n})$. This substantially improves upon the previously known logarithmic inapproximability bound. We also prove that \megset is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard on planar $2$-degenerate graphs, whereas $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness was previously known for $1$-apex $2$-degenerate graphs. We conclude by observing a connection between monitoring edge-geodetic sets and subsetwise distance preservers, i.e., subgraphs that preserve distances between all pairs of vertices in $S\subseteq V(G)$. Specifically, we show that any upper bound on the size of the latter yields a lower bound on the size of the former.

entry.title: An Exact Polynomial-Time Algorithm for the Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut Problem
entry.summary: The Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut (MSPEC) problem seeks to disconnect two designated terminals with minimum total power by assigning powers to graph vertices and deleting every edge for which the sum of the powers at its endpoints reaches its edge weight. Previous work gave a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem, while its exact computational complexity remained open. We prove that general MSPEC with nonnegative edge weights can be solved exactly in polynomial time. Specifically, we first use linear programming duality for each fixed cut to reformulate MSPEC as minimizing the maximum terminal-relaxed matching weight over all $s$-$t$ cuts. Then, we construct a terminal-copy extended graph that transforms the maximum-weight matching model with unconstrained terminal capacities for a fixed cut into an equivalent ordinary maximum-weight matching model. Next, we extend the submodularity of the unweighted maximum-matching cut function to nonnegative edge weights and prove that the restriction obtained by fixing the terminal copies on prescribed sides remains submodular. Consequently, MSPEC reduces to exact submodular function minimization. Once an optimal cut is obtained, a corresponding optimal power assignment can be recovered. This result resolves the open question concerning the exact computational complexity of general MSPEC.

entry.title: A 2/3-Approximation Algorithm for the Residual Maximum Matching Problem in General Graphs
entry.summary: The residual maximum matching problem asks for a maximum matching whose deletion leaves a graph with the largest possible matching number. For unweighted graphs, previous work provides a $1/2$-approximation guarantee in general graphs and a $2/3$ guarantee in graphs with a perfect matching. We present a $2/3$-approximation algorithm running in $O(n^5)$ time, extending the latter guarantee to general graphs. The algorithm improves the residual matching number through single-edge exchanges involving free vertices. We prove that, for any maximum matching that admits no further improvement by such exchanges, the residual matching number is at least $2/3$ of the optimum, and we give an example showing that this bound is tight.

entry.title: Improved rapid phase ordering for Ising dynamics on random regular graphs
entry.summary: We study Glauber dynamics for the Ising model on random $d$-regular graphs with $n$ vertices at low temperature, in the regime $β\geq C/d$ where $C,d$ are sufficiently large constants. In this regime, the full mixing time is exponential in $n$, because of the bottleneck between the two dominant phases: configurations with a majority of plus spins and configurations with a majority of minus spins. We show that, for sufficiently large $d$, if the dynamics is initialized with an excess of at least $ε_{C,d} n$ plus spins over minus spins, then it quasi-equilibrates in time $O(\log n)$ to the Gibbs measure conditioned on positive magnetization. In addition, the required bias $ε_{C,d}$ can be chosen so that $ε_{C,d}\to 0$ as $d,C\to\infty$. Previous bound of \cite{GSS25+} in the Ising and large-$d$ setting required $β\gtrsim (\log d)/d$. A key difficulty is that, even from the all-plus initialization, one must control the propagation of negative information in spacetime in a low-temperature model with strong local correlations. We address this by developing a new bootstrap approach to proving subcriticality of disagreement clusters under the grand coupling.

entry.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
entry.summary: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.

entry.title: Approximating Directed Telephone Multicast
entry.summary: In the telephone model a message starts at a source vertex, and in every round each informed vertex may call one neighbour. Telephone multicast asks for a schedule that informs a given set of $k$ terminals in the fewest rounds. On directed graphs, the best known ratio for this problem was $\tilde O(\sqrt k)$, due to Elkin and Kortsarz and to Hathcock, Kortsarz and Ravi. For every integer $\ell\ge2$, we give a deterministic combinatorial algorithm with running time $n^{O(\ell)}$ that computes a schedule of length $O(\ell^3\log k)\cdot(\mathrm{OPT}+k^{1/\ell})$, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $\mathrm{OPT}$ the optimum. Since $\mathrm{OPT}\ge\log_2(k+1)$, this gives ratio $O(k^ε)$ in time $n^{O(1/ε)}$ for every fixed $ε>0$, and ratio $O(\log^4k)$ in quasi-polynomial time. The method rests on jump trees with additive vertex loads, a height reduction that bounds the load of every vertex, and a recursive greedy algorithm with an exponential potential. We also show that directed multicast is a special case of the degree-bounded directed Steiner tree problem on a time-expanded digraph. With known algorithms for that problem this gives randomized ratios $O(\log^2n)$ in time $n^{O(\log n)}$ and $O(n^ε)$ in time $n^{O(1/ε)}$, which, unlike ours, grow with $n$. On the hardness side, directed multicast stays $(1-ε)\ln k$-hard even when $\mathrm{OPT}=O(\log k)$, the regime in which the previous algorithms were weakest.

entry.title: Communication Complexity of Universal Features
entry.summary: Motivated by the notion of features from machine learning, we study the complexity of representing data that allows for evaluation with a given family of functions. Concretely, we consider a deterministic encoder that observes $X\sim D$ and produces a finite encoding before a task $f\in\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is specified. For each task, a decoder must predict $f(X)$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ under $D$. We construct an encoder that outputs a representation with $O(d^{*}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits, where $d^{*}$ is the dual VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. Our encoder greedily selects $O((d^{*}/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ functions from the class and uses their joint label pattern to produce the encoding. The key idea in our upper bound is a novel potential function argument, where we compare the entropy gained from each greedy selection with the number of patterns allowed by the dual VC dimension. We present lower bounds showing that the representation length achieved by our encoder is worst-case optimal for every $d^* \ge 1$ and $\varepsilon < 1/4$ up to a universal constant factor, and instance-wise optimal for every family $\mathcal{F}$ up to an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ factor. We give two ways to learn the representation from unlabeled samples, with different guarantees on the representation size and sample complexity. Experimentally, we verify the greedy construction's accuracy-size tradeoff and explore its connection to neural sparse autoencoders.

entry.title: Parameterizing Cluster Editing by the Number of Deletions
entry.summary: In Cluster Editing, we are given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$ and ask whether at most $k$ edge insertions and deletions turn $G$ into a disjoint union of cliques. Komusiewicz and Niedermeier asked in 2012 at MFCS whether Cluster Editing is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number $\ell$ of edge deletions, a parameter based on the solution rather than on the structure of the input graph. We answer this question negatively: Cluster Editing with at most $k$ edits, at most $\ell$ of which are deletions, is W[1]-hard with respect to $\ell$, even when combined with the pathwidth and the feedback edge set number of the input graph. The hardness extends to editing towards $H$-free graphs for every graph $H$ that is a clique minus one edge on at least four vertices. On the positive side, we show that the problem becomes fixed-parameter tractable when $\ell$ is combined with the excess $μ$ of $k$ over the lower bound given by a packing of modification-disjoint induced paths on three vertices, a lower bound that state-of-the-art solvers use. Each of the two parameters alone leads to intractability, but together they admit an $O(4^{μ+\ell}\cdot(n+m+μ))$-time algorithm and a problem kernel with $O((\ell+μ)^2)$ vertices. Both results extend to packings of stars and the algorithm extends to $H$-free editing.

entry.title: Optimal Algorithms and Hardness for Max-Cut in Bounded Degree Graphs
entry.summary: We give a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $α_{GW} + \tildeΩ(1/d)$-approximation for Max 2-LIN(2) in weighted instances where each vertex appears in at most $d$ constraints. This improves on the $α_{GW}+\tildeΩ(1/d^2)$-approximation guarantee of [Hsieh-Kothari, ICALP'23]. We also show a matching Unique Games hardness under randomized polynomial-time reductions, thereby proving that the gain on $α_{GW}$ is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors. Here, $α_{GW} \approx 0.878$ is the approximation ratio of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm. Our results resolve an open question due to Raghavendra and refute his conjectured optimal approximation ratio of $α_{GW} + \tildeΩ(1/\sqrt{d})$. Our local improvement scheme can be thought of as using an adaptive (based on the neighbors) shift applied to the Gaussian before using the GW sign rounding. This allows us to implement a ``soft but simultaneous'' flipping decision at each vertex as opposed to hard but sequential flipping decisions in prior works. Our hardness results are based on a new sparsification lemma for graphs produced by the reduction from Unique Games [Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, SICOMP'07] that preserves the optimal values up to a factor of $1 \pm ε$ while subsampling to an average degree of only $\tilde{O}(1/ε)$. This is the first example of a CSP in which the optimal advantage on degree-$d$ instances is asymptotically smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ [Trevisan, STOC'01]. A key idea in the proof of our sparsification theorem establishes new bounds on the number of ``nearly optimal'' cuts in the output of the KKMO reduction. This step, in turn, relies on a new, robust inverse Majority-Is-Stablest theorem.

entry.title: Deterministic Shift Equivalence Testing for Sparse Polynomials
entry.summary: We study the shift equivalence testing problem for high-degree sparse multivariate polynomials. Given explicit spar se representations of two polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with exponents encoded in binary, sparsities $s$ and $t$, and total degree at most $d$, the task is to decide whether there is a vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ such that $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a})\equiv g(\mathbf{x})$. Furthermore, one needs to output such a vector if it exists. Dvir, Oliveira, and Shpilka (ICALP 2014) studied shift equivalence for low-degree arithmetic circuits. Their framew ork does not apply directly to sparse polynomials, which are not closed under shifts, and they left open whether shift equivalence of sparse polynomials admits an efficient deterministic algorithm. We answer this question positively over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the input coefficients have bit-size at most $τ$, we sh ow that a rational shift of polynomial bit-size exists whenever the polynomials are shift equivalent. Moreover, our alg orithm outputs such a shift and has a running time of $\operatorname{poly}(n,s,t,τ,\log d)$ in the bit model. The ar ithmetic and structural parts of our result also hold over any field of characteristic zero or characteristic larger th an $d$.

entry.title: A Short Note on Algorithms For The Noisy $k$-XOR Problem
entry.summary: This mostly expository note studies the sample-noise regimes in which the testing problem for noisy $k$-XOR in dimension $n$ can be efficiently solved. Concretely, we ask what pairs $(β, δ)$ admit algorithms running in time $n^{O(k)}$ where $m = n^β, β\in [0,k]$ is the number of samples and $\mathsf{Bern}(n^{-δ}),δ\in (0,+\infty)$ is the noise distribution. The current state-of-the-art algorithms are: I. A folklore algorithm when $β> 1, δ>1$ based on Gaussian elimination; II. A folklore algorithm when $β\ge k/2$ based on the birthday paradox; III. A recent algorithm in the regime $β> δ+ k(1-δ), δ\in (0,1)$ based on a reduction to the first algorithm [DJ24,CSZ24]. IV. Extending [AF09], we strictly improve the last regime to $β> δ+ (k-1)(1-δ), δ\in (0,1).$ These algorithms correspond to efficiently finding short cycles in uniform hypergraphs and can be equivalently phrased as algorithmic Moore bounds.

entry.title: A simplified proof of the FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
entry.summary: We give a simplified, self-contained proof of OpenAI's FPRAS for counting perfect matchings in general graphs. As in the original proof, we use a restricted Poincaré inequality for two matchings to sample weighted perfect matchings and estimate their total weight. We simplify the proof of this inequality by isolating parts of alternating cycles directly on the original vertex set and controlling the resulting error terms. This avoids the auxiliary vertices and tree constructions used in the original proof. The argument preserves the required parameter bounds and yields the same FPRAS guarantee.

entry.title: A Tight Oracle Threshold for \(k\)-Submodular Maximization
entry.summary: We prove that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), a \((\frac{k}{2k-1}+\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for maximizing monotone \(k\)-submodular functions requires exponentially many value-oracle queries. This improves the \(\frac{k+1}{2k}\) oracle bound of Iwata, Tanigawa, and Yoshida. Their \(\frac{k}{2k-1}\)-approximation algorithm therefore gives the exact threshold in the monotone setting. For \(k\ge5\), our bound also matches, up to an arbitrarily small loss, Aggarwal's recent approximation guarantee for non-monotone \(k\)-submodular maximization.

entry.title: Capacitated Line Aggregation with Maximum Delay
entry.summary: We study capacitated line aggregation with per-batch maximum delay. Requests arrive over time at locations on a rooted half-line and are served in instantaneous batches of at most $k$ requests. Each batch pays the distance to its farthest request plus the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is to minimize the total cost. We give a deterministic online algorithm with competitive ratio $36+12\sqrt3$. The algorithm uses a Next Fit idea along paths of nested time intervals: it assigns a new group to an existing batch when a path-load test permits, and opens a new batch otherwise. The path load controls both capacity and the cost of opening new batches. Randomizing the common scale improves the expected competitive ratio to $(18+6\sqrt3)/\ln2$ against an oblivious adversary. Both guarantees extend to arbitrary indivisible request sizes. We also study capacitated LAD in the learning-augmented model. Advice revealed at its service times allows $(1+ε)$-consistency against every complete feasible advice schedule and $O(ε^{-2})$-robustness. The analysis charges repeated switches to successive decreases in the remaining advice cost.

entry.title: Orienting mixed graphs for reachability pairs: When the all pairs setting is easier than the general one
entry.summary: Given a mixed graph $G$ and an ordered pair $(u,v)$ of vertices in $V(G)$, we say that an orientation $\vec{G}$ of $G$ satisfies $(u,v)$ if $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $\vec{G}$. We consider problems in which we seek orientations that satisfy a maximum number of pairs. We distinguish between two different problems. In the most general problem called Fixed Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (FPRO), a multiset $P$ of ordered pairs of vertices in $V(G)$ comes with the input. In the more restricted problem All Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (APRO), $P$ contains exactly one copy of every ordered pair of distinct vertices in $V(G)$. We compare the computational complexity of FPRO and APRO in two ways: First, we show that both FPRO and APRO behave similarly when it comes to approximation. Namely, they both admit an asymptotic approximation, but are unlikely to admit a constant factor approximation. Then, we consider the parameterization with respect to the treewidth of the underlying graph of the input mixed graph. We show that here the complexities of FPRO and APRO differ significantly. While it is well-known that FPRO is NP-hard even when this parameter is 1, we show that APRO is XP with respect to this parameter. On the other hand, we give a $W[1]$-hardness result for APRO.

entry.title: Constructive Arithmetic Regularity for Abelian Groups
entry.summary: The arithmetic regularity lemma of Green is a fundamental tool in additive combinatorics, providing a decomposition of arbitrary subsets of finite Abelian groups into pseudorandom pieces with respect to Fourier analysis. Over the years, it has found numerous applications in combinatorics, property testing, and theoretical computer science. However, Green's proof is existential, and many algorithmic applications require an efficient procedure for constructing the underlying regular decomposition. De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio (SODA 2022) developed a query-efficient constructive regularity framework over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and explicitly raised the problem of extending their dimension-independent sumset-estimation algorithm to other finite Abelian groups. In this work, we resolve this question for finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. We develop the first constructive version of Green's {\em Arithmetic Regularity Lemma} in this general setting. Given oracle access to a subset of the group, our algorithm computes an implicit description of a regular decomposition together with an oracle representation of a structured subset satisfying the guarantees of Green's lemma. The algorithm runs in time and query complexity polynomial in the regularity parameters and the tower bound, while remaining independent of the size of the ambient group. As applications, we obtain efficient algorithms for removing linear configurations and approximately counting linear images, including weighted sumsets and suitable matrix systems of Cauchy--Schwarz complexity one, over finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. Our results provide a unified algorithmic framework extending dimension-independent constructive arithmetic regularity and its applications beyond $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

entry.title: Ski Rental with Uniform Stochastic Signals
entry.summary: Ski rental is one of the most fundamental online problems, where an agent repeatedly decides whether it should continue renting for a service, or buy it at a one-time fixed cost. In classic online analysis, an adversary may freely select any arbitrary time horizon $t$ after which the instance terminates, hence leading to strong competitive ratio lower bounds of 2 (deterministic) and $e/(e-1)$ (randomized). We consider a novel but natural model aiming at limiting the adversary's power without degrading its flexibility. A stochastic signal, containing no information apart from its arrival time, is transmitted to the algorithm at a time drawn from a known distribution scaled to $[0,t]$. This framework allows us to account for visible effects of the adversary's choice to the algorithm. Focusing as a first step on uniform distributions, we show that the best possible competitive ratios are approximately $1.478$ (deterministic) and $1.438$ (randomized). Surprisingly, simplistic deterministic strategies already achieve a performance of $1.489$.

entry.title: Dynamic $(Δ+1)$-Coloring Against an Adaptive Adversary: Faster, Simpler, Worst-Case, and Bounded Recourse
entry.summary: We study fully dynamic $(Δ+1)$-coloring against an adaptive adversary. Behnezhad, Rajaraman, and Wasim (SODA 2025) gave the first algorithm with $\tilde O(n^{8/9})$ amortized update time, later improved to $\tilde O(n^{2/3})$ by Flin and Halldórsson (ICALP 2025). We give a fully dynamic $(Δ+1)$-coloring algorithm with $\tilde O(\sqrt n)$ \textbf{worst-case} update time. Unlike previous algorithms, it avoids sparse-dense decompositions and relies only on elementary data structures, resulting in a short self-contained algorithm and analysis. Moreover, it avoids global recoloring, resulting in a worst-case recourse of $3$.

entry.title: Solving Classes of Linear Programs with Strongly Polynomial Straight Line Complexity in Strongly Polynomial Time
entry.summary: Recently, Allamigeon, Dadush, Loho, Natura, and Végh (ADLNV, SICOMP 2025) introduced an interior point method for linear programs whose number of iterations is bounded by the so-called straight line complexity (SLC) of the instance. This yields a strongly polynomial bound on the number of iterations of the corresponding interior point algorithm for broad classes of linear programs. In particular, in the companion paper we give a strongly polynomial straight line complexity bound for two-variable-per-inequality linear programs. However, in order to obtain a strongly polynomial algorithm for these classes, one also needs to address two important technical issues: initialization and bit-complexity bounds. Standard IPM initialization techniques either require numerical estimates that cannot be obtained in the strongly polynomial model, or involve modifying the instance in ways that do not preserve the geometry of the original LP, potentially affecting the SLC. In this work, we present an initialization framework for interior point methods for linear programming, along with a rounding procedure that ensures the continued feasibility of the IPM. We develop a multistage scheme in which each stage can be initialized in strongly polynomial time given the output of the previous stage. Additionally, we address the challenge of controlling the bit complexity of each iterate throughout the algorithm. To this end, we show that it is possible to represent iterates as low-complexity convex combinations of vertices and extreme rays. Our combinatorial rounding step is independent of the algorithm in ADLNV 2025, and can be applied more broadly in the context of path-following methods.
